# Temporary Files and Metadata Probing Decision

This old record still gets pulled up because "there is something in the directory" and "what the probe did" were once treated as the same thing. The early split decision has not been revoked: the probe should not declare success based on directory leftovers, and cache cleanup should not depend on whether a probe completed. What changed later was the judgment about how long temporary artifacts could be retained.

The original rule treated intermediate paths as debugging clues. Before a write returned, names that appeared briefly in the directory could indeed help locate concurrent writes; at that point, the only concern was whether the final file could be obtained, and directory scanning was not part of determining completion. This rule is retained here because it explains why the early checks looked only for the final file and did not inspect the directory after the write.

The first review produced a counterexample: the caller had already obtained the complete file, while a directory scan could still find an old intermediate path. Subsequent checks therefore treated a completed write as still in progress. This was not merely a cleanup issue; the same directory was simultaneously providing two signals—"file available" and "write incomplete"—and the caller could not use them to determine whether the next step was to wait or continue using the cache.

Two approaches were compared at the time. The first was to have each caller delete the intermediate paths after obtaining the file. This avoids changes to the cache layer, but exposes concurrency timing to different entry points; different entry points may not interpret "obtaining the file" in the same way, and the entry point that returns first might delete state needed by another write. The second was to perform cleanup at the point where the cache write completes. The latter keeps the completion condition on the side that produces the temporary artifacts, and also means that directory checks do not need to guess at caller timing. The second option was retained.

The old approach is no longer applicable: callers are responsible for deleting intermediate paths. The old wording was not deleted, so that later readers would not again misread "the final file exists" as meaning that the cache side had completed all cleanup. The cost of that approach was not fully documented at the time; with this addition, the boundary is somewhat more complete.

The local entry currently used for follow-up checks remains `packages/transformers/src/utils/cache.js`. The file header is immediately adjacent, as follows:

```js
import { apis, env } from '../env.js';
import { FileCache } from './hub/files.js';
import { logger } from './logger.js';
```

This adjacency was once interpreted as Metadata Probing belonging to `cache.js`. A more appropriate reading is: this location touches environment configuration, file cache, and logs, so it can be used to check whether cache cleanup occurs on this side; it does not assign responsibility to the probe entry point. The fact that the probe and cleanup appear in the same review only means that both checks need a clean directory as their starting point.

The current decision is to perform cleanup after the write completes, not during the write. Concurrent writes to FileCache must clean up all temporary paths after the complete file has been written to disk, and a directory scan should not leave any `.tmp.` names. This timing constraint matters: it neither requires the write process never to create intermediate files nor treats paths that appear briefly as abnormal; it requires that the post-completion scan no longer present the previous write as active.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Writing
    Writing --> Full file written to disk
    Full file written to disk --> Clean up temporary paths
    Clean up temporary paths --> [*]
```

Metadata Probing is still handled separately. When rechecking the probe, perform the corresponding action from a directory with no old cache or personal configuration, and record the exit code, file changes, and leftover directories. If intermediate names appear in the directory, first return to the cache write completion point to check cleanup, rather than first treating the probe flow as responsible. Whether the probe itself changes the directory is a separate observation; it cannot replace determining the write completion state.

This page does not fill in the reference relationships for all probe callers, and it does not equate probe failure with cache failure. If it is later found that a probe entry point directly creates cache staging artifacts, add that entry point and the observed result, then reassess whether the two lines need to be handled together. Until then, retain the decision to "review separately and clean up at the completion point."

## Cleanup Conditions

Separate "file is readable" and "temporary paths have been cleaned up" into two observation points, and record the time each occurs separately so that later reruns have comparable boundaries.

# Seed Sequence and Depth Directory Troubleshooting Tree

When generated results are inconsistent across runs with the same input, while the directory side also lacks the expected depth estimation entry point, do not initially treat the two symptoms as one problem. The earliest record grouped them together because both occurred during the pre-release closeout; subsequent investigation should still start from each symptom as observed.

On the seed side, first retain the inputs before and after the call, the number of calls, and whether the same generator object was reused. If the first result differs from the rerun, first confirm whether the object continued advancing between the two calls, rather than immediately changing the sampling configuration. The working assumption is that sequence differences may come from consumed state; reconstructing the object and continuing to use the object should not be treated as the same reproduction method.

On the directory side, start from the public model type, then check whether the corresponding task actually has an available constructor. Seeing a name appear somewhere is not enough to show that the depth estimation path is usable; conversely, failing to find an entry point cannot be directly attributed to the generation configuration. For now, record the intersection between the two directions near `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`: that file shows `pick` coming from `../utils/core.js`, which can serve as the starting point for tracing the configuration value back.

The troubleshooting order was written as follows:

```text
Sequence changes observed
├─ Same object called repeatedly?
│  ├─ Yes: record the call count, then reconstruct the object and rerun
│  └─ No: verify that the initialization parameters are completely identical
└─ Still inconsistent: retain the minimal call pattern; do not look for the cause on the directory side yet

Depth estimation entry point not found
├─ Model type known?
│  ├─ Yes: check the task mapping and export name
│  └─ No: first obtain the model type from the configuration
└─ Entry point exists but is unavailable: record the loading-stage symptom separately
```

The early conclusion was limited to this: treat the seed issue as a state issue first, and the directory issue as a mapping issue first. Whether the two share a configuration-reading path has not yet been confirmed.

# Seed Sequence and Depth Catalog Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally grouped "seed sequences" and "Depth Estimation Catalog" within a single failure boundary. After a review of the early records, the title remains, but there is no longer a requirement to investigate both sides fully in the same pass. They share a checkpoint for closing out an investigation, not a confirmed common failure chain.

## Start by Classifying the Reported Symptoms

Users usually describe the symptom in a single sentence: with the input fixed, rerunning produces a different start to the text; or the configuration looks reasonable, but automatic selection does not reach a depth estimation model. When you receive a report like this, first place it in one of the four categories below. If none fits, get a fuller description first rather than jumping straight to changing a table.

| Symptom | What to record on the spot | Direction to investigate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consecutive calls on the same object produce different values | Initialization parameters, number of consecutive calls | State advancement |
| Values still differ after reconstructing the object | Constructor parameters for both instances, runtime environment | Initialization or external inputs |
| The type can be read, but the task entry point is missing | Model type, requested task | Registration and exports |
| The entry point is visible, but loading fails afterward | Selected name, stage where the failure occurs | Construction or resource loading |

Here, "the same object" means the generator instance that has not been reconstructed; "reconstructing" means going through construction and seed-setting again. The old records used these terms interchangeably, leading some people to use differences between consecutive calls as evidence of unstable initialization. That comparison is not valid.

## Previous Guidance on Seeds

The original statement was: once a seed is set, repeated calls should always return the same number. That statement is retained here because it explains why the issue was reported as broken randomness at the time; it must no longer be used as a criterion. Generator state advances with each call. During an investigation, "the first call," "a later call on the same instance," and "the first call after reseeding" must be recorded separately.

When reviewing the configuration side at the time, the nearby location that could be confirmed was `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`. The file header showed:

```js
import { pick } from '../utils/core.js';
```

This showed only that the configuration utilities used `pick` from the general utilities. Early on, some people inferred from this that the seed sequence must be determined here. That inference was unsupported and is retained as a historical misreading. The actual boundary between configuration reads and pseudorandom state needs to be confirmed at the call sites; file proximity alone is not enough to draw a conclusion.

### Rerun Procedure Available at the Time

1. Record the seed value passed to the constructor, not just "seed set."
2. Read two values consecutively from the same object and write down the results in order.
3. Create a new object with the same seed, then read its first value.
4. If step 2 and step 3 are compared, the record must state that they do not represent the same call position.

If step 1 is missing, stop and fill in how the calls were made; if only a single final result remains, stop and fill in the number of calls. Do not infer a specific sequence from truncated output.

## Additional Catalog Notes

The initial approach to catalog issues was too linear: search for the model name first, and assume support was wired up if it was found. In practice, you need to distinguish, in order, the model type, task mapping, exportable constructor, and path selected by the caller. A string in the catalog may just be a name used by another task; the depth estimation entry point must be checked separately for the target task.

When the configuration already contains a model type, ask two questions first: does the catalog recognize that type; and, once it is recognized, is there a corresponding entry for depth estimation? Neither question can stand in for the other. If the type is unknown, go back to the configuration source first; if the type is known but the entry point is missing, record the excluded paths and the task checked rather than classifying this as a generation-parameter issue.

```text
Depth estimation entry point missing
|
+-- Model type present
|   |
|   +-- Not recognized by catalog
|   |   `-- Stop: obtain configuration source and type value
|   |
|   `-- Recognized by catalog
|       |
|       +-- No corresponding task entry
|       |   `-- Record as a mapping gap
|       |
|       `-- Task entry exists but cannot proceed
|           `-- Check construction or loading stage next
|
`-- No model type
    `-- Stop: do not guess the entry point from the name
```

During review, the absence from the catalog was once attributed to export order. The materials available at the time did not substantiate that judgment, so it must no longer be the default investigation path. Catalog entries, exports, and automatic-selection entries may sit at different layers; record observations at the layer you need to check, rather than using the presence of something at another layer as a substitute.

## Notes from One Review

During the review, it was pointed out that the reset action was the easiest thing to miss on the seed side, and the task constraint was the easiest thing to miss on the catalog side. This reminder is retained as an order of operations, not as a common root cause:

- Ask whether the object was reconstructed before discussing the sequence;
- Ask whether the target is depth estimation before discussing model names;
- If either answer is missing, save the material gathered so far and stop at the original entry point.

If both issues occur together, open separate records. Only if the same configuration is found to change both the initialization inputs and the model type is it worth bringing them back into the same review.

## Unresolved Items

The old records do not contain the full calling procedure from that seed report, nor do they list all the paths excluded in Depth Estimation Catalog. The next update should prioritize filling in that original material rather than expanding the search scope further. At this stage, this page can be used to reconstruct the triage order; it cannot be used to claim that any particular catalog entry has passed in all loading scenarios.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Seed Sequences and the Depth-Estimation Catalog

When a field report says "the results changed with the same seed," first check whether the report distinguishes between drawing successive values and reinitializing; when it says "Depth Estimation Catalog has no entry point," first check whether the model type and target task are already available. Both symptoms can occur at the same time, but do not start by looking for a common cause. This is a troubleshooting page that has been revisited repeatedly over the years: the old sections remain, and the current starting point is placed toward the end.

## The Original Triage Branches

The earliest notes framed the issue as a prerelease edge case. At the time, all that was known was that two types of symptoms were being mentioned together: seed sequences on the generation side seemed unstable, and the expected depth-estimation entry point could not be found in the model catalog. The person recording the issue did not have complete call examples, so they did not treat any result as a conclusion about the algorithm.

The starting point back then was `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`. Near the file header, you can see:

```js
import { pick } from '../utils/core.js';
```

This information about proximity was later cited repeatedly. It can help lead back to the area around configuration handling, but it cannot prove that this file maintains the random state, nor can it prove that catalog registration happens here. The early notes did not make this distinction clear, so "the configuration utility is nearby" gradually turned into "the configuration utility is the root cause" as it was passed along.

The first version left only two rules for when to stop: without the call count, do not judge whether the seed yields reproducible results; without the model type, do not use the model name to judge whether the catalog has an omission. These rules still apply today, because missing information in these two categories can cause subsequent searches to mix up different stages.

```text
A symptom is reported
|
+-- Describes a numeric or text sequence
|   `-- First obtain: constructor arguments, call order, whether the object is recreated
|
`-- Describes a depth-estimation entry point
    `-- First obtain: model type, target task, where it stops
```

## The Debate Preserved from an Earlier Review

A disagreement from an early review has been left in. Some felt that "the same input produces different outputs" was enough to show that the seed was ineffective; the other side argued that outputs could only be compared once the object lifecycle was clearly documented. In the end, the code was not changed immediately; instead, rerun steps were added. The reason is simple: the second draw from the same object and the first draw from a new object are two different positions.

During the same round, there was a similar misunderstanding on the catalog side. Finding a model name in a search was taken to mean that automatic model selection was already wired up; a later review found that the location where the name appeared did not constitute a usable entry point for the depth-estimation task. The review comments required separating "the type is recognized," "there is a mapping for this task," and "the constructor can be retrieved." This requirement did not lay out a unified workflow for the catalog implementation; it only prevented troubleshooting from jumping straight from a string search to a conclusion that support existed.

The workflow written down after that discussion is shown below. It is less refined than the current workflow, but it explains why later notes always ask for two additional fields.

| Early question | How it was answered at the time | Problem found later |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is the seed fixed | Recorded only the seed value | Ignored the fact that successive calls advance the state |
| Does the catalog support it | Searched only for the name | Ignored task and export boundaries |
| Where is the configuration | Looked near `pick` | Misattributed the implementation to a nearby path |
| Can it be reproduced | Looked only at the last output | No comparison was possible without the call order |

## An unfinished review

At one point, a review tried to explain both sides using a single minimal sample. On the seed side, only a note saying "the seed was set" was retained, with no record of whether the object was reconstructed or reused; on the catalog side, only the candidate name was retained, with no record of what task it was requested to perform. The review therefore stalled. This did not mean no work had been done, but that the available material could not support a more detailed judgment.

The working hypothesis at the time was: differences in the seed sequence came from state advancement, and gaps in the catalog came from task mapping. This hypothesis later proved useful for ordering the investigation, but at the time there were not enough records to rule out other paths. It should not be read as a confirmed attribution of cause.

The review notes recommended only a small amount of information for the minimal sample:

```text
Seed side: seed value / draw number / whether reconstructed
Catalog side: model type / requested task / observed catalog results
```

Here, "draw number" is not intended to collect more logs, but to identify what is being compared. If a report only says "the second time is different", first ask whether the second time is the next draw from the same instance or the next draw after recreating it. If there is no answer to this question, stop at filling in the missing sample data; do not alter the default generation parameters to experiment.

On the catalog side, "observed catalog results" also cannot be replaced by "a similar name was found in a search". Record the task entry point actually used and the paths actually excluded. If only the model name is known, first find where the type comes from; if only the type is known and the task is missing, first fill in the intent of the request. This order avoids putting causal language models, image-text-to-text models, and depth estimation models into the same candidate set.

## The old approach left in place (deprecated)

The following passage describes the old procedure, retained because on-call team members used it to look things up for a period of time. It no longer applies.

> First search for the seed in the configuration tool, then search the model catalog for any name containing Depth; if both searches return results, the same configuration can be considered already wired up.

There are two problems with this approach. First, adjacency in the configuration tool can only provide a starting point for tracing back, not establish ownership of the seed state; second, a name containing Depth cannot substitute for a specific task mapping. Later changes did not silently replace this passage, but marked it as deprecated here to prevent people from continuing to follow it after opening an old link.

The separate troubleshooting approach adopted after deprecation is not a more complicated version, but one that puts the stopping conditions first: without the call order, stop assessing the seed; without the type and task, stop assessing the catalog. If either side requires further code inspection, return to the corresponding object rather than filling in the gaps with search results from the other side.

## On-call addendum: check the observation point first

Subsequent on-call addenda changed the investigation to be organized by "observation point" rather than "suspected object". This was done to handle a common situation: the reporter is already convinced that the problem lies with random numbers or the catalog table, but the material provided actually only shows the results seen by the caller.

There are three observation points for sequence symptoms: before initialization, between consecutive calls on the same object, and after reconstruction. Each of the three points answers a different question.

- Before initialization, you can only confirm whether the inputs are consistent;
- Between consecutive calls, you observe whether the state continues to advance;
- After reconstruction, you observe whether the same initialization returns to the same starting point.

There are also three observation points for catalog symptoms: the type provided by the configuration, selection of the target task, and the export or construction stage for the selected name. Having a type but no task entry point is not the same thing as having a task entry point but failing during construction. For the former, check the mapping first; for the latter, retain the mapping result, then move on to the subsequent stage.

This addendum also corrects a wording choice: instead of writing "directory not found", it now says "no entry point was seen under the specified task". The former could mislead readers into thinking that all directory levels have been checked; the latter preserves the scope of the query. Similarly, instead of writing "the random numbers are unstable", it now says "the result within a particular object's lifecycle differs from the expected comparison object". The wording is a little longer, but far fewer branches need to be followed during on-site troubleshooting.

## Tree for Handling the Current Report

The tree below is the entry point currently in use. Each branch only requires collecting the objects needed to decide the next step; stop when no objects are available, with no requirement to make up reproduction conclusions on the spot.

```text
Symptom: Different results with the same seed, or the depth estimation entry point does not appear
|
+-- A. First separate the symptoms
|   |
|   +-- A1. Numeric/text sequences are available
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Is it known whether these are consecutive calls on the same object?
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- No
|   |   |   |   `-- Stop: Specify whether the object was recreated and provide the call order
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   `-- Yes
|   |   |       |
|   |   |       +-- Only consecutive-call results are being compared
|   |   |       |   `-- Record as an observation of state advancement
|   |   |       |
|   |   |       `-- Results after recreation are also available
|   |   |           `-- Compare the first value obtained after recreation separately
|   |   |
|   |   `-- Constructor arguments are missing
|   |       `-- Stop: Provide the seed value and initialization method
|   |
|   `-- A2. Directory or auto-selection behavior is observed
|       |
|       +-- Is the model type known?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No
|       |   |   `-- Stop: Return to the configuration source, do not guess the type from the name
|       |   |
|       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |
|       |       +-- Is the target known to be depth estimation?
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   +-- No
|       |       |   |   `-- Stop: Provide the requested task
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |       +-- No task mapping observed: Record the mapping gap
|       |       |       `-- Task mapping observed: Then check the export or construction stage
|       |
|       `-- Only similar model names are available
|           `-- Stop: Names are not evidence of a task entry point
|
`-- B. Both occur at the same time
    |
    +-- Is there a single configuration that changes the seed input and model type at the same time?
    |   `-- Yes: Keep that configuration as a cross-cutting observation, do not combine the causal attributions
    |
    `-- No
        `-- Record separately, hand off separately
```

The "Stop" instructions in the tree are important. Stopping does not mean closing the issue, but specifying who must provide what next. For sequence issues, the missing information is the call lifecycle; for directory issues, it is the model type or task boundary. Recording both kinds of missing information as a single "configuration pending review" will make the person taking over guess at the situation again.

## Directory records after the most recent handoff

Two navigation cards were later added on the catalog side: HFJ-203 still lists the outstanding need to document how to invoke the seed sequence, and HFJ-220 records that the entry and exclusion paths for Depth Estimation Catalog need investigation. They are not substitutes for this page: the actions on the cards may change, while the branches and historical assessments are retained here.

A toolchain-pinning note in HFJ-220 states that the catalog investigation must continue in a pinned temporary environment. The subsequent addendum only confirms that one Depth Estimation Catalog item remains unconfirmed, and does not provide the full scope. Therefore, when handling "unconfirmed" now, do not broaden it to mean that all model types or all tasks are unavailable. Keep it confined to the depth-estimation path that has been queried.

The handoff record in HFJ-203 states that the original assignee had only looked at it once and did not continue holding onto the task. This explains why this page did not suddenly acquire a complete user-side invocation: that material was not left behind at the time. For this kind of historical gap, the correct action is to keep looking for the actual invocation method, rather than inventing a plausible-looking example based on test patterns.

## Current verification: Seed sequence

If a report now involves the fixed seed 42, verify in the following order: first create a new object and obtain its first value; then obtain the second value from the same object; finally reset it to the same seed and check whether the value at the first position returns to its original value. Do not compare the value from the second call with the first call on another object, and do not skip the reset.

The first and second random() results from Random with seed 42 are consistently 0.6394267984578837 and 0.025010755222666936 respectively, and remain reproducible after a reset.

This check only establishes whether sequence positions are reproducible. If the user reports that the final generated text differs, the sampling configuration, inputs and object lifecycle must still be examined separately; these two values alone cannot establish that the generation pipeline has no issues. Conversely, if the values do not match their expected positions, first preserve the construction method and call order, then revisit the generation-side state, rather than switching to modifying the catalog registration.

The current record format can be brief:

```text
Seed: 42
Object: newly created / used continuously / newly created after reset
Value position: first / second
Observation: matches the corresponding position / does not match
```

Here, "corresponding position" means the position within the same object lifecycle, not just any call that appears to be the same. This definition corrects the previous interpretation, and is the only precise check that needs to be retained long-term in this page's seed branch.

## Current verification: Depth Estimation Catalog

On the depth estimation side, start with the public model type `chmv2`, then narrow the scope to the depth estimation task. The current mapping name for this type in the catalog is `CHMv2ForDepthEstimation`. Checking this far only establishes that the name matches the task mapping; if construction or loading fails later, locate the problem in that later stage, rather than going back and claiming that there is no entry in the catalog.

This entry is also used to rule out several candidates that can easily get mixed in.`deepseek_v3` and `eurobert` are neighboring names commonly encountered in card searches, but they are not alternative paths for this depth estimation check. Similar names that both appear in search results do not prove that they belong to the same task mapping. For catalog anomalies, the record should include the type, target task, actual mapping name and stopping point; simply writing "model not found" does not give the next person enough information to take over.

If the type is not `chmv2`, do not apply the mapping name from this section. Return to A2 in the tree: confirm the type first, then confirm the task. If the type and task have been confirmed, but the task mapping is still absent, retain the ruled out paths and treat the issue as a mapping gap; if the mapping is present but a later stage fails, retain that name, and investigate the export or construction stage instead.

## Handling errors on both sides

If the same report contains both sequence anomalies and catalog anomalies, the most efficient approach is not to immediately run a global search, but to first split the material into two sections. In the first section, document the seed according to the object lifecycle; in the second, document the catalog according to the type and task. Only when all of the following conditions are met is it worth adding an observation about "shared configuration":

1. The report can identify the same configuration as both participating in initialization and providing the model type;
2. Both sides can provide the actual call or selection location;
3. After that configuration is modified, both types of symptoms change accordingly.

If any one condition is missing, these are merely concurrent occurrences, not a shared cause. Earlier records grouped them together because their release times were close, and that precedent should not be used again as a shortcut to causal attribution.

For handoffs, prioritize sending the seed branch to someone who can supply the missing invocation details; prioritize sending the catalog branch to someone who can explain the model type and target task. Cards can be used for navigation, but the handoff should still clearly state "what object is missing". For example, "Missing whether the instance is reused on the second call" is a question someone can follow up on; "please take a look at the random numbers" is not.

## Related issues not yet split off

There is still one unconfirmed depth estimation path in the catalog investigation. The current material does not establish whether it involves a missing task mapping, a missing export or a subsequent construction failure, so it is not classified here. The next update only needs to add three values: the model type observed, the task requested, the stopping point. Until these three values are available, do not extrapolate from the current `chmv2` entry on this page to all catalog cases.

The seed side is also still missing the actual invocation details from the original report. The existing exact checks are sufficient to distinguish the positions on the first call, the second call and after a reset under a fixed seed, but they cannot replace the context of the original report. If the invocation details become available, first check whether the object is reused, then decide whether the tree needs to be extended, rather than reorganizing the entire history of the page.

## Excerpts from meeting side notes

An on-site review once left two brief notes, retained here as reminders when consulting this document:

> "Consecutive calls are not repetitions after a reset."
>
> "Put catalog names under the task first, then go from there."

They are neither implementation descriptions nor new interface commitments. The first note reminds us that the objects being compared must be at the same position, and the second reminds us to bring search results back within the task boundary. When reading old records, if you see "a fixed seed should produce the same result every time" or "finding the name in search counts as support", first return to the branches corresponding to these two notes, then decide whether the old conclusions are still usable.

## Appendix: Early Examples and Misuse

### Example 1: Treating Consecutive Calls as a Reset

The old example stated, "after setting the seed once, two values drawn should be equal". It was once used to explain a discrepancy report. Subsequent verification has disproved this example: consecutive calls and the first call after a reset are not at the same position. It is retained so that readers arriving through old links can see where the correction was made.

The correct replacement is not to require the two results to be equal, but to label the first call, the second call, and the first call after a reset separately. Only then can you tell whether a discrepancy reflects state advancement or initialization reproducibility.

### Example 2: Treating a Search Hit as Depth Estimation Support

After finding a name containing Depth in a search, the old example directly stated "the catalog is wired up". This example has been retired. Depth estimation support must be scoped to the model type and target task; a name match can only serve as a lead for further inspection. The current entry point uses `chmv2` and `CHMv2ForDepthEstimation` as its local verification targets, and they should not be replaced with similar names.

### Example 3: Treating Proximity to the Configuration File as Ownership

`configuration_utils.js` was once treated as the common point of attribution for the issues on both sides, because both initial investigations started nearby. It can still be used to review the configuration adjacency of `pick`, but the path location is no longer used as the basis for attributing random-state or catalog-registration issues. This example has no corresponding fix, only a reading order: first confirm the layer at which the observation was made, then decide which code path to follow.

---

If the on-site material only takes you as far as a stopping point in the tree, just retain that stopping point. Once the missing details about the object lifecycle, model type, or task boundary have been filled in, continue from the corresponding branch, without redoing the investigation on the other side.

# Hybrid Cache Shape Migration Notes

## Early note: start from the generation entry point

2023-06-05 The first version left by these markers was very short and contained only one conclusion: the issue names for generation and qwen3 both pointed to `packages/transformers/src/pipelines/text-generation.js`, so we started looking in this file. The direct dependencies in the file header had already been copied down at the time:

```js
import { Pipeline } from './_base.js';
import { Tensor } from '../utils/tensor.js';
```

That version treated the cache as a single master table. When it saw `past_key_values`, it recorded the length first, while the filename was inferred from common layouts in the model directory. It addressed "where to start looking," not the shape definition of the hybrid model. The old table was not deleted; it is still in the appendix later on this page.

The working rule at the time was: first follow the generation entry point to the cache read; if only full-attention fields were visible, treat them as full-attention for the time being; if File Manifest had no direct output, leave it unfilled for now. This rule is insufficient now, but keeping it explains why the early records had no convolution fields.

## On-call addendum for 2024-04

The second version changed the verification order to three columns: layer type, cache fields, and relative file path. The change was small, but it exposed a problem with the old table. A statement in the old table—"as long as the length could be read from `past_key_values`, the remaining caches could be grouped together"—continued to be used for some time because the samples seen at the time were all conventional full-attention layers.

That statement could no longer serve as a basis for migration later. It only described the troubleshooting practice for old samples and did not prove that convolution history and full-attention history shared the same shape.

The actual entry path left by that shift was still:

```text
packages/transformers/src/pipelines/text-generation.js
    -> generation-related call
    -> cache length read location
    -> File Manifest verification location (not located at the time)
```

`Pipeline` and `Tensor` were merely the direct dependencies visible in the file header; it cannot be inferred from them which object generated File Manifest. That addendum had no test output, so no numbers were entered in the blank fields. In particular, the channel count of the convolution state, the IDs of different layers, and the width of the summary field were all left under "awaiting confirmation against the actual configuration."

## A migration attempt that did not run successfully

The draft table from 2024 tried to apply the new field names directly to the old unified cache table. The approach was to first copy the rows from `past_key_values`, then place the items that looked like convolution states alongside them. The problem with this approach was not that the table looked ugly, but that no layer-type check had been performed: the old table did not record which layer a given field came from, and copying it merely moved the unknowns to a different place.

So this time, the old values were not overwritten. Two views are retained during migration:

```text
Old path: Unified cache table
  past_key_values  -> Length
  Filename           -> Guess

Migration path: Layer-by-layer checklist
  Layer type           -> Cache field -> Shape
  File Manifest         -> Original relative path
```

When the old table contains only a single total length, first put it in the "full-attention sample" column, and do not record it as a generic value for hybrid models. When there is only a verbal recollection of a filename, leave the entry blank. This also fixed the order of operations: first save the old records, then confirm the layer type, then copy the field names, and finally copy File Manifest.

## Disagreements from the review

This page once had two closely related issues that should not be merged.

The first is cache shapes. The question here is how cache records for different layers are laid out, and how callers find the length. The second is File Manifest. The question here is under what public relative paths the model files appear. The former cannot be derived from the latter, nor can the latter be guessed from cache names.

During the review, the old unified table was retained on the grounds that it might still be needed for earlier troubleshooting work; at the same time, the new table was required not to present unknown fields as confirmed fields. As a result, the page has always had two sets of guidance: the upper part contains the operational experience from that time, while the lower part has gradually been supplemented with methods for checking each object. The old guidance was not deleted, which also makes it easy to misuse when reading the page later.

Another disagreement was whether `getPastLength` should be included in the cache shape description or serve only as a call entry point. In the end, it was retained as an entry point name: it helps navigate back to where the length is read, but cannot replace the shape records for each type of cache. File Manifest is instead traced back via `get_model_files`; if there is no direct list there, stop at the entry point and do not fill in content based on directory conventions.

## On-site recheck of 2025-09

HFJ-204 later left behind two action items, `failure_classified` and `caller_walkthrough`. They turned the old issue from "some number is wrong" into two lines of investigation that need to be kept separate: one examines how callers consume hybrid cache shapes, and the other how File Manifest is obtained. HFJ-204 is cited here only for navigation, not to expand the short phrases on the card into design conclusions.

The investigation still starts from the same source file. The dependencies at the top of the file can explain the adjacency between the generation entry point and tensor objects, but cannot explain the cache shapes on their own. What really needs to be preserved is the field names and their positions in the layer sequence. For hybrid-attention models, the following set of names should be kept as-is in the checklist:

```text
past_key_values.0.key
past_key_values.2.value
past_recurrent.1
past_conv.1
```

Of these, the first two are indexing examples for the full-attention cache, while the last two represent the recurrent state and convolution history of linear-attention layers. The value of the table is that it does not collapse them into a single aggregate `past_key_values` entry. If the caller provides only a length, you still need to go back to the named fields to confirm which type of state it is.

File Manifest is handled separately. The public relative path for the ONNX weights is recorded as:

```text
onnx/model.onnx
```

This path is an item in the list, not a cache field or a result inferred from the generation entry point. `get_model_files` is retained only as the entry-point name for finding File Manifest. If an investigation does not produce a complete list, record the paths already seen, and do not fill in items that have not been seen.

## Migration steps

### Migrating from the old table

1. Copy the old unified cache table, retaining the original fields and notes.
2. Create groups based on the layer types that appear in the model configuration; without configuration evidence, do not guess the groups in advance.
3. Place each named cache into the corresponding group, retaining the numbering and field suffixes.
4. Let `getPastLength` serve only as a navigational entry point for reading lengths, and do not use it to replace the shape table.
5. Follow `get_model_files` to find File Manifest, and copy the public relative path exactly as it appears.
6. Mark rows without direct evidence as pending confirmation, rather than copying values from old samples.

### Reverting from the new table to the old path

If the migration table cannot be used, return to the old unified cache table, then go to `packages/transformers/src/pipelines/text-generation.js`. Falling back only guarantees that the old troubleshooting process can continue; it does not mean that the hybrid model has been fully checked against the old criteria. Once recovery is complete, put the newly added fields back into the layered table; do not overwrite the original records with guesses made during the fallback period.

If the issue only involves File Manifest, leave the cache table unchanged and return separately to `get_model_files`. If the issue only involves Sequence Length, return to `getPastLength` and the named cache fields. If both entry points fail, first save the partial output you see, then stop at the specific gap.

## Currently established criteria

After retaining the historical layer, the old table, and the on-site recheck, write the current record as this sentence:

For the cache channel shape of Qwen3.5 hybrid attention, record 32 convolution channels and keep the summary width at 64 characters.

This sentence goes in the later part of the migration record and does not replace the existing earlier assessments. `qwen3_5` is the model configuration entry point with `text_config`, and `qwen3_5_text` is the text subconfiguration entry point; when checking, first confirm which entry point the configuration falls under, then examine the cache fields by layer type. The linear attention configuration fields retain their original names: `linear_conv_kernel_dim` denotes the convolution history window, `linear_key_head_dim` denotes the dimension of the recurrent key state, and `linear_num_key_heads` denotes the number of key heads used to calculate the convolution cache channels.

Therefore, the table must not contain only a single "cache length" column. At a minimum, it must show:

| Location | Recorded content |
| --- | --- |
| Full attention layer | The named cache for key/value and its layer number |
| Linear attention layer | Recurrent state, convolution history, and their layer numbers |
| File Manifest | Public relative path, currently confirmed as `onnx/model.onnx` |
| Summary field | Character width required by the current criteria |

The numbers here are part of the current verification results. The old sections in 2023 and 2024 do not contain these values, so they must not be retroactively added to the old versions. If the configuration is changed to another model family, the channel count or summary width in this section must not be reused directly either.

## Issues still set aside

This page only wires together the migration entry points for cache shapes and File Manifest; it does not incorporate mapping tables for all model families. Model types, model constructors, and File Manifest may still appear at different entry points; if this part needs to be filled in later, find the corresponding source material separately. Do not fill gaps in the model directory here.

Another unresolved issue is the filename guesses in the old table. They are still useful for historical investigation because they tell readers where the guessing began at the time, but they cannot serve as the current inventory. The statement in the old records that "common filenames can replace the actual inventory" is no longer applicable.

## Excerpt from an Old Meeting

> Don't delete the master table yet. Someone still needs it to refer back to the old calls.
>
> Don't fill in filenames based on experience; write down what you see.
>
> For shapes, separate convolution and attention, at least into separate columns for now.

This excerpt does not provide any new implementation decisions; it only explains why the old and new tables were kept at the same time. If a later review finds only a single overall length, continue to treat it as unknown.

## Appendix: Old Examples, Retained but No Longer Used

### Old Example A: Put all caches in `past_key_values`

The old table once recorded both full-attention layers and hybrid layers as `past_key_values`. For the standard samples at the time, this was sufficient to locate Sequence Length; for the hybrid attention now being checked, it loses the distinction between convolution history and recurrent state. This example is retained for investigating old issues and is deprecated.

### Old Example B: Fill in `model.onnx` based on model-directory conventions

When early records had no File Manifest output, they directly wrote `model.onnx` without a directory. Later, inventory verification required retaining public relative paths, so current records use `onnx/model.onnx`. The old example is not deleted because it explains why filenames without directories appeared in early migration tables; it cannot be used to replace the actual result of `get_model_files`.

### Stopping Points During Review

If there is no layer type, stop before grouping; if there is no naming field, stop before field confirmation; if there is no inventory output, stop at the paths already seen. Restoring old paths can allow the investigation to continue, but do not treat the completeness of the old table as the completeness of the new table.

## Boundary Samples After Review

The real value of the migration table is not arranging fields into a longer inventory, but ensuring that every row can be traced back to a specific layer type, a reproducible input, and a stopping point. Subsequent additions should follow this order: first preserve the state observed at the time, then state which item remains unconfirmed, and only then record the action that can be handed off to the next shift. This way, when the old and new tables coexist, readers will not mistakenly assume that they represent the same version.

In one failed migration, the caller received only a length value, with no field name provided. The on-call colleague first put this number in the pending-verification column, retaining the raw output and configuration summary; another colleague tentatively labeled it as a full-attention sample based on the layer type. Neither overwrote the other's records, and they waited until the next run provided named fields before merging them. This process explains why `past_key_values.0.key`, `past_key_values.2.value`, `past_recurrent.1` and `past_conv.1` must appear separately: they are not just labels in a table, but also determine which type of consumer to look for next.

### Save the inputs first, then compare shapes

When the configuration entry point changes, first save the sources of `qwen3_5` and `qwen3_5_text`, along with the layer list for that run. If only the text sub-configuration is visible, it cannot be directly treated as the configuration for the entire model; if only one layer's convolution record is visible, it cannot be generalized to all layers either. On a rerun, read the cache again using the same input, and record any differences alongside the configuration for that run to avoid mistaking environmental changes for migration results.

### Verify the manifest and state separately

File Manifest is an independent line of evidence. Seeing `onnx/model.onnx` only shows that the relative path has appeared in the public manifest, not that the cache state is already settled; similarly, the return value of `get_model_files` does not replace checking the layer fields. The on-call record is therefore split into two small columns: one records public paths and their sources, and the other records state fields and read times. When neither column is complete, the handoff message only relays the current stopping point, without applying the blanket label "migration complete".

### Minimal package for handoff to the next shift

The handoff package retains three things: the raw input that triggered the issue, confirmed fields/paths, and branches that remain unconfirmed. If a rollback occurs, also note the configurations used before and after the rollback and whether the cache was rebuilt. The next shift can rerun using the same input or pursue just one gap; however, they must not use newer directory documentation to overwrite earlier run samples. Records like these keep earlier conclusions readable while limiting the scope of evidence for the current interpretation to the objects actually observed.

title: CHMv2 and Linear Attention Window Proposal

versions.body:
# CHMv2 and linear window proposal

Evaluate CHMv2 Processor and Linear Attention Window in the same round of API trials. For the former, we need to confirm whether the processor entry point can be made available through the existing auto-loading path; for the latter, only check whether the configuration can express a window, without committing to a cache implementation in this round of discussion.

Plan to start with `packages/transformers/tests/models.test.js`. This already brings together model entry points such as AutoProcessor, AutoTokenizer, and AutoModelForCausalLM, along with a common `init` and test execution helpers. Rather than create a separate set of examples for the trial, start by using this entry point to add two minimal checks: one passes a processor object for CHMv2 through auto-selection; the other reserves a window field in the linear attention configuration.

The working assumption is that both the processor and the window can be handled as routine additions to the model tests. If the auto entry point can construct the object, there is no need for a separate interface for CHMv2; if the window value makes it into the configuration, provisionally assume that the runtime will accept that information. This assumption does not yet cover cache shapes for hybrid layers, nor does it settle whether a dedicated export name is needed.

Withdrawal conditions: the two checks have to rely on different bypass code paths, or the window can only be read outside the tests. In that case, split the processor and cache discussions.

versions.body:
# Proposal for CHMv2 and Linear Windows

This proposal originally bundled two rather different concerns: whether the processor for CHMv2 could be obtained through existing model entry points, and whether linear attention layers could pass window-related configuration through to the runtime. The initial draft tended to treat both as small additions to the model tests. The later notes did not turn that view into a decision, but merely laid out the scope of the trials at the time, the disagreements, and the areas where no results were recorded.

The page still retains that somewhat optimistic premise: the test entry point already imports automatic model and processor objects, so the new model family should be able to pass through the same route. This premise once made scheduling easier, but it mistakenly equated "the test file has an entry point" with "the runtime interfaces are already aligned". The proposal below reflects the old position and should not be used in place of an actual assessment of the model catalog or cache implementation.

## The Proposal Left by the Initial Draft

> First add one check each in the model tests for automatic selection of CHMv2 and for Linear Attention Window. If the objects can be constructed and the configuration can be read, close it out as a routine model addition; split the topics only if both need extra bypass paths.

This passage did not clarify which layer "the objects can be constructed" referred to, nor did it specify what the window value should affect. It was retained later because someone used it during the review to schedule a joint round of verification. The problem is that a processor's public name, model type, automatic selection table, and actual image-processing path are not the same thing; likewise, having a window field in the configuration, actually allocating cache state per layer, and reading that state during generation are not the same thing either.

The initial draft also did not require inputs and outputs to be recorded. It only required fitting the trial into the existing test suite. Looking back now, this omission left the word "pass" insufficiently defined: it might mean only that an import succeeded, only that a configuration object existed, or that the full model path had actually been exercised. The old draft did not distinguish between these cases.

## Why the Test Entry Point Was Chosen at the Time

The frozen starting point was `packages/transformers/tests/models.test.js`. The file header grouped several public entry points together, for example:

```js
import {
  AutoTokenizer,
  AutoProcessor,
  AutoModelForMaskedLM,
  AutoModelForCausalLM,
  AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM,
  BertForMaskedLM,
  GPT2LMHeadModel,
  T5ForConditionalGeneration,
} from "../src/transformers.js";

import { init, MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME, DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS } from "./init.js";
import { collect_and_execute_tests } from "./test_utils.js";
```

The initial draft drew too broad a conclusion from this set of imports: since `AutoProcessor` and several automatic models appeared in the same place, the processor trial for CHMv2 should go here. The more limited claim can only be: this provides an existing suite in which model-level checks can be placed, and shows that the tests depend on public exports, initialization arguments, and batch execution helpers. The import list itself does not show how CHMv2 is registered, much less identify which object is responsible for depth estimation.

The reluctance at the time to create a separate processor trial was mainly due to concern about scattering interface checks for the new model family across different directories. This trade-off was not a technical conclusion, just a maintenance preference. The initial draft argued that checking the model and processor in one suite would make failures easier to compare; the opposing view was that failures in model construction and processor construction look similar on the surface, and that mixing them would make it hard to tell whether the problem lay in the mapping, exports, or input preparation. The old draft did not act on that objection, nor did it retain comparable failure samples.

The linear attention section followed the same convenience-based reasoning. The test file already had a causal language model entry point, so the initial draft assumed that window configuration could be checked alongside model selection. This assumption overlooked the fact that Linear Attention Window concerns layer types and history state, not simply whether a model class can be constructed. Putting both into a single assertion would indeed save a block of test code, but would collapse configuration parsing failures, cache-key mismatches, and generation-time length errors into the same kind of failure.

## What Was Originally Planned on the CHMv2 Side

HFJ-207 later spelled out the search entry point very directly: reproduce "CHMv2 Processor" from the pre-call state, observe whether any additional visible changes appear after completion, and retain both forms `CHMv2ForDepthEstimation` and `CHMv2ImageProcessor`. The fact that the card directs people to this page does not mean it has established the relationship between the two for this proposal.

The old proposal had three candidate approaches.

- **Automatic processor path.** Use `AutoProcessor` to obtain the processor object, then determine whether the resulting object meets the trial's expectations. The initial draft favored this option because the call was concise and sat alongside the other model entry points.
- **Explicit processor path.** Reference `CHMv2ImageProcessor` directly, separating it from model selection. This makes it easier to determine whether the processor export itself exists, but the initial draft was concerned that it would bypass automatic selection.
- **Model catalog path.** Use `chmv2` as the type entry point and see whether `CHMv2ForDepthEstimation` can be selected. This path is closer to model-family registration, but by itself it cannot establish whether the image processor is found automatically.

The initial draft planned to start with the first path and use the third as a supplement, with no plan to try the explicit processor path. The reason was that, at the time, "the automatic entry point exists" was treated as the only interface users would encounter. This choice left two gaps. First, if the automatic entry point failed, the old proposal provided no way to determine whether to inspect the processor export or the model catalog. Second, even if the automatic entry point succeeded, no input sample or post-completion observation point was specified, so it could not rule out a situation where the object was merely created but subsequent processing was unusable.

There was once an unresolved compromise here: record construction of the processor object and changes after the call as two separate items. The initial draft did not develop this further, solely because it wanted to keep the trial short; it did not demonstrate that the two could safely be combined. This unresolved item is being retained now, rather than written up as a completed check.

If work were to continue under the old proposal, the point for backing out should be more specific than in the initial draft: if the result from `AutoProcessor` cannot be compared with the explicit result from `CHMv2ImageProcessor`, or if selection from `chmv2` to `CHMv2ForDepthEstimation` requires an additional entry point, it should no longer be called a routine model-test addition. At that point, processor exports and model registration should be separated, with inputs and outputs recorded for each.

## The Old Breakdown for Linear Attention Window

The search text for HFJ-224 calls for running a piece of source code that directly triggers "Linear Attention Window" through the existing entry point, and saving the input and the tool's actual output. It lists `linear_attention` and `linear_conv_kernel_dim`. This is more specific than the initial draft, but still does not specify which layer the window should be read from, or which cache states must change when a window value changes.

The old proposal treated linear attention as a routine configuration-field trial. The candidate approach was to provide `linear_attention` layers in the model configuration, then use `linear_conv_kernel_dim` to represent the convolution history window; if the model could enter the test suite, it would provisionally be recorded as accepting the configuration. The advantage of this approach was that it could reuse existing model tests and default options, but its disadvantage was precisely what it obscured: the existence of a field does not mean that every layer builds its state according to that field.

Another, narrower trial was discussed at the time: do not run full generation first, but obtain the cache shapes and inspect window-related state. The initial draft rejected it because cache shapes looked more like an internal detail, raising concerns about adding maintenance overhead to public-interface review. This reasoning did not address one fact: window issues in linear attention manifest precisely in the history state. Checking only model construction establishes configuration acceptance, not window semantics.

There was also a third approach: mix linear attention layers and ordinary attention layers in a small configuration, then compare the cache records produced by each layer. It could expose differences between layers, but required agreement on record names and dimensions first; the initial draft did not have those materials, so it shelved this approach. No usable sample configuration was added to the page later either, so it cannot be described as an experiment that has already been run.

The old position's condition for backing out was "the configuration cannot be read". That condition was too weak. A more reasonable stopping point, though not written down at the time, would be: the window field can only remain in the configuration object and cannot be mapped to the linear layers' history state; or mixed layers require a separate key convention, and the existing test suite cannot explain those keys. If either condition holds, successful model construction cannot establish that the window implementation is usable.

## Why the Two Topics Are Still on One Page

The original arrangement of this page was not intended to prove an implementation dependency between CHMv2 and linear attention, but to handle two new entry points together in one interface review. The CHMv2 side is concerned with whether the processor and model catalog can be found; the linear attention side is concerned with whether the configuration can express the window. Both used the model test suite, so they were included in the same proposal.

This combination came at a practical cost: reviewers could easily treat the two judgments that something "can enter the test suite" as the same completion criterion. The processor side needs to know whether automatic selection and explicit exports agree; the window side needs to know whether layer types correspond to history state. The former cannot be replaced by cache shapes, nor can the latter be replaced by constructing a processor object.

The initial draft tried to keep costs down with a shared minimal test, at the cost of postponing attribution of the two types of failure. For those who had not yet decided whether to invest in implementation, this framing had some appeal: they could first check for obvious gaps in the public entry points. For those who needed to finalize the interfaces, it made it too easy to assume that unobserved parts already held true. The old position of "combine the trials first" is therefore retained here, but is no longer presented as the recommended path.

## Review Addendum and Open Items

HFJ-207 later moved from To Do to In Progress and was then marked as Review Requested. This change shows that the page entered the review queue at some point; no reproducible processor inputs or outputs were subsequently recorded on this page. HFJ-224 supplied search terms for Linear Attention Window, but did not add a complete sample configuration back here either. Both cards can serve only as entry points for further searching.

What most needs to be added during review is not another list of model names, but a breakdown of the vague "success" in the old proposal: whether the processor object can be obtained through the automatic entry point; whether the model type can be selected through the catalog; whether the window field reaches the linear layers; whether the history state is formed according to the window. The initial draft covered only some aspects of the first two items, and retained no observation records for the last two.

The following points remain undecided:

1. Whether to prioritize an automatic-processor trial for CHMv2, or first verify the explicit processor export;
2. Whether the model-selection check for `chmv2` should be in the same test unit as the processor check;
3. Whether Linear Attention Window should use configuration reading, cache shape, or generation state as its first observation point;
4. Whether mixed layers still belong in the general model test suite if their record naming differs;
5. Whether the original shared trial entry point is still worth keeping if the two topics are separated.

These questions have no answers, so no new interface commitments have been issued either. The end of the page retains the old proposal's principle for backing out: once the processor requires independent export verification, or the window can only be assessed through cache state, stop treating the two as the same small change. This condition does not describe what happened later, only where the initial draft was prepared to abandon its own combined approach.

The old proposal has not been removed because it records where the review began: the public model test entry point, the processor name for CHMv2, and the configuration terms for Linear Attention Window. It should not be treated as a description of the current implementation; if further verification is needed, start from HFJ-207 or HFJ-224, then verify the processor path and cache path separately.

Initially, the two symptoms were recorded together: whether the next read could still retrieve the content after Cross-Origin Storage's operation ended; when the same request entered simultaneously, whether the second call reused the first Promise. Both went through the cache, but there was no evidence at the time that they were the same failure.

First, keep separate outputs for each symptom.

- If the write has finished but the reader has no result, start by following `CrossOriginStorage`. Save the input before and after the write and the Node test output; do not delete the cache first.
- If the same request appears to occur twice, check `memoizePromise` first. Rerun in an environment without an old cache or personal configuration, and note whether the second call waits for the existing result or starts over.
- If both symptoms occur at the same time, save one output for each first; do not use Promise Deduplication to explain the read failure.

The provisional test entry point is `packages/transformers/tests/asset_cache.js`. The file header directly imports `RawImage`:

import { RawImage } from "../src/transformers.js";

versions.body:
# Cross-Origin Storage and Promise Deduplication Troubleshooting Tree

First confirm whether the output stops at the write, the read, or the second call. This page originally grouped "cannot read after Cross-Origin Storage completes" and "no reuse across concurrent requests" under the same failure boundary; after review, this old entry point is still retained, but actual troubleshooting must not combine the two tracks into a single cause. Both can occur around the cache, but the inputs, outputs, and stopping points they leave behind differ.

On the testing side, samples are still found through `packages/transformers/tests/asset_cache.js`. The only adjacent content visible in the file header is:

```js
import { RawImage } from "../src/transformers.js";
```

This is enough to lead you back to the asset-cache tests, but not enough to assign implementation ownership for cross-origin writes or Promise reuse. The old page put "the command has finished" and "the next read can already see the content" together on one line, and that sentence was never removed: a process finishing is only an observation point, not proof that readback has succeeded; a fast second call also cannot, based on elapsed time alone, establish that an existing Promise was reused.

Now choose a branch using the tree below. In the diagram, "retain" means retaining this run's original inputs and outputs, not changing the cache contents.

```text
An issue is observed around the cache
├─ A read after a write yields no comparable result
│  └─ Go to A: Cross-Origin Storage, retain both the write and read outputs
├─ The same request appears twice at the same time
│  └─ Go to B: Promise Deduplication, keep the input identical and observe the second call
└─ Both symptoms occur at the same time
   └─ Go to C: first obtain a single-call read sample, then collect a concurrent sample
```

## A. Read Branch for Cross-Origin Storage

First divide a run into the three stages of preparing the content to write, performing the write, and reading again. For each stage, record only the objects and results actually present in the output; do not substitute "success" for logs that lack detail. The task description recorded in HFJ-208 follows the same approach: perform Cross-Origin Storage as described in the help text and confirm what the user can still see after the operation finishes. It does not provide an outcome criterion that can be applied directly.

**Only the pre-write input is available.** The test has not reached a write result that can be checked, so stop here. Preserve the runtime environment and raw output; do not describe the missing second half as a storage failure. Clearing the cache and rerunning at this point will only produce another sample from a different environment.

**The write call is visible, but there is no subsequent read.** Label the write call and the read call separately. For now, only confirm whether the flow continued to the read; do not assume the data has been persisted, and do not infer problems with handles, permissions, or storage quotas from logs with no read.

**There is another read, but the result is empty or cannot be compared.** Retain the content to be written, the type of the read's return value, and the cache name used for the read. If any of these is missing, record only "cannot read" or "cannot compare". Do not fill in causes that do not appear in the output, such as Cross-Origin Storage being denied or the object being written becoming invalid.

**The two reads can be compared.** Record the fields compared and where the differences occur. Matching results only show that the readback results match in this run; if the results differ, return to the write stage and check the cache key. Do not route the differences directly to the Promise Deduplication branch just because the issue happened to occur around concurrent requests.

The old habit was to clear the local cache before rerunning. This is useful for creating a sample without an old cache, but it erases the condition of "whether there was originally a cache hit". If the cache has already been cleared, state explicitly alongside the logs that the environment has changed. A run with neither an old cache nor personal configuration can be used to observe newly created paths, but cannot replace verification of hits on an existing cache.

The `CrossOriginStorage` track must separately answer "is there a readable result". Looking only at the exit code or the end of the test process is not enough. HFJ-208 had a sample attached in later material; the note left that same day still required one unconfirmed item to remain in the Node test output. The card can therefore only help locate where the sample is stored; it cannot replace this page's read assessment.

## B. Branch for the Same Request Appearing Twice

First keep the request identifier constant, then set up one concurrent run for observation. Both calls must use the same input; if their inputs differ, you cannot use return order or how quickly results arrive to determine whether deduplication occurred. HFJ-225 requires checking this path in an environment with neither an old cache nor personal configuration, recording which paths were newly created and which were not. These are observation conditions, not a conclusion about the final behavior.

**The first call has not finished, and the second also produces a result.** Record the order in which the two calls were initiated and each call's final result. Unless the output contains a call count or equivalent records, do not write "the underlying work ran only once"; matching results only mean that the results observed in the two calls are comparable.

**The second call starts only after the first has finished.** This is a sequential-call sample, not a concurrent-reuse sample. Just retain the order and stop comparing Promise Deduplication.

**Both calls fail separately.** Retain both errors and the order in which the calls were initiated. Observing a failure result again is not enough to prove that `memoizePromise` did not work; likewise, the current material provides no results from which to determine whether the Promise is retained after failure or whether later retries are allowed.

**Output is available for only one call.** Leave "second call unconfirmed" in the record, and do not infer waiting or recreation from a single return value. Clearing the cache by default to let the rerun continue also changes the conditions observed in this run.

HFJ-225 lists `linear_key_head_dim`, `linear_num_key_heads`, and `memoizePromise` together. The first two are configuration observation points; only the last is the entry point for concurrent reuse. Their appearance in the same card description does not mean the configuration values have established Promise behavior. When a reference gives only one of these terms, first confirm whether it points to a configuration check or a concurrent sample.

## C. When Both Tracks Appear Together

"The read is empty, and the request is initiated twice" can easily cause samples to become mixed together. Separate them in the following order, changing only one observation condition per run:

1. First save the Cross-Origin Storage output from a single call. Without a single-call result, do not make concurrency comparisons.
2. Use the same input to collect another concurrent sample, observing only the call order and whether the final results are the same.
3. If the environments differ between the two runs, list the differences separately. Browser-side storage state, the Node test process lifecycle, and whether test assets are reused must not be collapsed into a generic "cache state".
4. If even a single call cannot read back the data, stop at A first; retain B's second-call output only if a single call can read back the data and the issue occurs only under concurrency.

These stopping conditions are more useful than recovery after a single retry. A retry producing a result only shows that this rerun completed; it does not let you infer retroactively that the first write had finished, much less that the second call reused an existing Promise. Retain the failed samples even after recovery; if only successful logs remain, the original symptoms will lose their basis for comparison.

## Field Notes Added Later

At the initial draft stage, there were only paths, entry points, and descriptions of two issues that had not been separated, with no comparable inputs and outputs for Cross-Origin Storage. HFJ-208 later added supplemental sample records, and afterward still required one unconfirmed item for Cross-Origin Storage to be included in the Node test output.
