# Dynamic Cache Probe Strategy Migration Notes

## Preserve the old entry point first

This work initially used issue names and invocation names to locate files, eventually landing on `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`. The only content currently verifiable directly in the file header is this line:

```js
import { pick } from '../utils/core.js';
```

It shows that `configuration_utils.js` has a direct dependency on `../utils/core.js`. It does not show that `DynamicCache` is created here, nor does it list the callers. The v1 working hypothesis—that Dynamic Cache and Probe Cache Policy may share an entry point in this area—remains as a historical assessment, but is no longer treated as evidence that migration is complete.

The first thing to migrate this time is therefore the verification order: change from "an issue name or invocation name points to a file" to "record the observed state first, then cross-check against local declarations in the file". The input provides neither a new target file nor specific callers or command names. A path that has not been provided must not be filled in as the migration destination.

## Pre-migration state

Before the check begins, the working directory must contain no old cache and no personal configuration. This condition keeps "newly created" and "not newly created" distinguishable as two observations. If the directory already contains an old cache, seeing an existing path does not show that this check created it; if personal configuration changes the default behavior, an identical record from another environment cannot be directly placed alongside this result either.

During preparation, record only the conditions, without drawing conclusions in advance. The record can begin like this:

```text
Old cache: None / Unconfirmed
Personal configuration: None / Unconfirmed
DynamicCache: Awaiting observation
Probe Cache Policy: Awaiting check
```

"Unconfirmed" must not be written as "None". If the preparation conditions themselves were not recorded, file inspection can still continue afterward, but this result must be kept separate from a baseline that meets the conditions. Cleaning the working directory is preparation for the next round of checks, and must not retroactively become evidence that "the check left no residuals".

## First branch: DynamicCache

The `DynamicCache` branch answers only whether the cache object or its corresponding path has changed. Preserve three possible observations: newly created, not newly created, and different results across the two checks. The third case must not be reduced to "cache exists", because it shows that the same observation did not produce the same result under different conditions.

This branch is not responsible for explaining the probe check's exit result or proving the source-code entry point. Even if a newly created path is observed, it can only be recorded as part of the observed state; the file must not be identified as its creator merely because an earlier investigation pointed to `configuration_utils.js`. Conversely, if no file changes are observed, that does not justify recording that the cache was not used: no file changes and no cache activity are not the same observation.

When recording DynamicCache, at least keep the observed object and its result together, rather than leaving an isolated word:

```text
Observed object: DynamicCache
Result: Newly created / Not newly created / Different from the previous check
Working-directory file changes: Record separately, do not include in the result above
```

"Working-directory file changes" here still describe the observed state; they are not another way to write the DynamicCache result. Only when both items are recorded can a later comparison determine whether "cache object changes" and "directory changes" occurred together; if only one is recorded, the other remains unrecorded.

## Second branch: Probe Cache Policy

Check Probe Cache Policy separately, rather than combining it with the first branch into a single "cache is working normally" result. The actual command for this check does not appear in the frozen material, so use only the check's name when recording the entry point, without inventing a command, arguments, or an exit code.

This branch must preserve three distinct results: the exit code, file changes in the working directory, and residual directories after the check completes. The exit code indicates only the return result of that check process; it cannot replace directory observations. Directory changes do not mean the check failed either, while residual directories require a separate record of their names or "present/absent"; do not invent names when the material provides no specific directory names.

The observed state can be saved in exactly the following order:

```text
Probe Cache Policy
  Exit code: To be recorded
  File changes: To be recorded
  Residual directories: To be recorded
```

If only the exit code is available, mark the other two items as unrecorded; if only a clean working directory is observed, the exit code must not be filled in as successful either. In particular, cleanup performed after the check does not justify treating the post-cleanup directory state as the state immediately after the check ended. To compare before and after migration, all three observations must retain their respective positions in time.

## Do not merge the two paths

The current verification order can be drawn as a branching path:

```text
No old cache, no personal configuration
              |
        Record preparation conditions
          /           \
Observe DynamicCache       Check Probe Cache Policy
Newly created/Not newly created/Result changed      Exit code
                          File changes
                          Residual directories
          \             /
             Review the local file
                 |
configuration_utils.js + pick dependency
```

There is only one shared prerequisite before the fork, and each branch preserves its own results afterward. When the branches rejoin, only compare them; do not combine them into a single conclusion. For example, DynamicCache not being newly created does not automatically mean that the probe strategy left no residual directories; a normal probe exit result does not automatically mean that DynamicCache must have been newly created either. The material provides no causal relationship between these two items.

If only one branch is completed during the check, leave the other branch's entries blank in the document. Completing the DynamicCache observation does not mean that Probe Cache Policy has been verified; completing the probe check does not mean that the old file entry point has explained the cache behavior either. Recording things this way preserves the differences needed for the next comparison better than filling in a single "compatible" result.

## Migrate from the old path to an observation-first sequence

The old path has the advantage of making the file easy to find. Its drawback is equally specific: issue names and invocation names can lead someone to a related file, but cannot by themselves prove that the object is created by that file. The new sequence does not remove the old path; it places it after the observations instead.

First, confirm the environmental conditions and register blank entries for DynamicCache and the probe check. Second, perform both observations and save their results separately. Third, return to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js` and verify only the currently visible local declarations and the `pick` dependency. Fourth, place the observed results and file adjacency information side by side; if there is insufficient material to connect them, stop at side-by-side records rather than extending them into a call chain.

This has another practical benefit: when new results conflict with an old assessment, it becomes possible to see whether the conflict is at the observation level or the file-location level. If the observation for DynamicCache changes while the file header still contains only the same direct dependency, that change cannot be interpreted as a change in which file the implementation belongs to. If the file entry point can still be found but the probe check's residual directories differ, the file's existence cannot be recorded as evidence that behavior is unchanged either.

"Migration" here means migrating the verification entry point and recording order, not that source-code relocation has been completed. New implementation paths, a list of callers, and specific recovery commands do not appear in the material, so this page does not assume that they exist.

## How to incorporate the existing baseline

HFJ-209 recorded `baseline_recorded` on 2025-09-23. This record is suitable as a starting point for comparison: later observations must not overwrite it and then pass off the new results as the original baseline. At a minimum, the baseline must retain the conditions and observations actually written down at the time; do not use the action name "baseline_recorded" to infer the result for DynamicCache.

By 2025-09-26, the action for HFJ-209 had changed to `work_started`. What can be confirmed here is that verification had moved from baseline recording into the working phase; this does not justify filling in a probe exit code, file changes, or residual directories. If those results were obtained later, create a separate observation record and place it alongside the baseline.

When incorporating this batch of records, distinguish the purposes of the two points in time:

```text
baseline_recorded
  Purpose: Mark the starting point for comparison

work_started
  Purpose: Mark when verification resumed

Subsequent observations
  Purpose: Enter the actual observations from both branches
```

Action names are not behavioral results. They can help reconstruct the order of records, but cannot replace engineering facts such as whether a cache was newly created or whether probing left directories behind. If the baseline recorded only DynamicCache, do not backfill it from a later probe check; if the baseline did not record environmental conditions, do not assume that it necessarily used a clean directory either.

## Caller compatibility boundaries

The material provides no specific callers, new files after migration, or integration points in external projects. This page therefore specifies only the observation granularity that callers must support: if a caller reproduces DynamicCache, it should be able to distinguish newly created, not newly created, and changed results; if a caller runs the probe check, it should be able to record the exit code, file changes, and residual directories separately.

This is not proof that callers have completed the switch. When a caller returns only final success or failure, at least the directory and residual information is lost, and the result cannot be compared directly with the old baseline. When a caller reports only that the directory did not change, that does not justify asserting that no cache activity occurred either. If such a difference occurs, save the raw output first, then identify which item is missing.

Do not extend the file-header dependency in `configuration_utils.js` into an end-to-end relationship. Currently, all that is known is that `pick` is a direct dependency; it is not known who calls the file or whether it receives or creates DynamicCache. If new code snippets appear later, place them under the corresponding local branch; a new name cannot replace the complete reference relationship.

## Fall back to the old entry point

When the new sequence cannot be followed, the fallback action is to locate the original file again, not to delete the observations already recorded. If cross-checking still leads to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`, retain the `pick` dependency in the file header as a local anchor, and note beside it which observation was not completed.

If DynamicCache has already been observed but Probe Cache Policy has not yet been checked, return only to the second branch; do not mark the second branch as passed merely because the first has a result. If neither branch has a result, return to environment preparation and establish the baseline again. If the probe check has been completed but the residual-directory record is missing, fill in only that item during fallback; the post-cleanup directory state must not replace the original observed state.

Restoring the old path guarantees only that the original local entry point can still be found, not that the v1 working hypothesis holds again. The file location from the old investigation can still be referenced, but must not be promoted to the conclusion that "the implementation is right here". Retaining the old records of file changes, exit codes, and residual directories is also important; the next check needs to know which material was left from the previous round and which observations are new.

## Conclusions currently retained

The confirmed points are: the DynamicCache observation and the Probe Cache Policy check should be separate; the old-cache and personal-configuration conditions must be made explicit before checking; the probe branch records the exit code, working-directory file changes, and residual directories separately; the old investigation can be traced back to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`, whose file header directly shows the `pick` dependency; HFJ-209 first recorded a baseline and then entered the working phase.

The unconfirmed points are also retained: whether the file creates DynamicCache, whether a new migration target file exists, which callers have switched, whether the probe strategy produces a consistent result across environments, and whether the baseline included all environmental conditions at the time. Subsequent material should go into the corresponding observation, source-code, or caller section. Without new material, do not combine these gaps into a single compatibility conclusion.

versions.body:
# Decision on OCR Mapping and Cache Keys

At the time, OCR Mapping and Cache Key Shape were included in the same round of requirements review for a simple reason: both surfaced before model loading as "a name or state mismatch." Grouping them made investigation easier, but was not a sound basis for planning the implementation. When a name does not resolve to a loadable model, cache-shape results cannot establish that the mapping is complete; when the keys in a cache record do not match the caller's expectations, they cannot be used to infer which entry is missing from the model catalog either.

The initial working hypothesis was that both issues might stem from the same omission in the model declarations. To check this, the notes retained only `packages/transformers/src/models/trocr/modeling_trocr.js`, a nearby entry point opened at the time. It helps locate the local declarations again, but the path name cannot establish that OCR Mapping, the model catalog, and the cache state share an implementation location. This counterexample made the earlier assumption that "one change could close out both" untenable.

Three approaches were compared at the time.

- Combine the two issues into one change request and close it only after both the mapping and cache checks pass.
- Fill in the model names first, then treat cache-shape checks as accompanying validation for that change.
- Keep two separate acceptance checkpoints: verify the mapping by the model-type-to-constructor result, and verify the cache by whether its named keys can be consumed.

The decision was to use the third approach. This does not mean the two have no runtime connection; it avoids using a passing result on one side to vouch for the other. The OCR item records only whether model types, task entry points, and exported names are consistent; the cache item records only whether the names, indices, and shapes of each layer's state can still be read. If a change touches both, they can appear together in the commit description, but the regression record must distinguish which acceptance checkpoint a failure belongs to.

The proposal to "generate unified cache-key documentation from the OCR model file" was also deferred at the time. Model mapping is a catalog-level selection, while cache keys come from the state layout; putting the latter into the mapping table would make the name table responsible for explaining runtime structure, making it harder to determine the scope of changes when hybrid attention layers are added later. Cache-key documentation should stay near where the state is actually consumed, while model mappings should keep type-to-constructor relationships searchable.

This page retains an older framing that now looks too narrow: OCR Mapping was treated only as a single missing name, with no record of the differences in entry points after the model family was expanded. It still helps explain why acceptance checks were split at the time, but should not be treated as the complete rules for the model catalog. In subsequent investigations, first confirm the registration result for the specific model type, then check whether the corresponding cache keys are still read by the caller.

## Boundary between mappings and keys

Model family names locate registration entries, and cache keys describe runtime state; when both appear together, investigate each using its own evidence.

# Nemotron and Olmo Exception Troubleshooting Tree

This record originally placed Nemotron and Olmo side by side under a single troubleshooting entry point. This worked for collecting exception names that appeared sporadically during the prerelease stage, but later review required separating "checked in the same round" from "following the same implementation path". The former still holds; the latter cannot be inferred from the existing material.

The file currently available for direct review is `packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js`. Its name, imported objects, and test time limit are enough to show that it is a checkpoint for reviewing a specific part of Olmo2; it cannot establish the missing links to tests for Nemotron. When investigating, first document the exceptions by stage, then decide whether to look at this file. Do not jump straight to a "shared fault" based on similar model names, inclusion in the same prerelease version, or appearance in the same regression round.

The approach left in the early records was: open the Olmo2 test first, then look for the construction stage after finding the model import. This approach can still be used to locate symptoms on the Olmo side, but cannot serve as the first step for Nemotron. The original branches are retained below, with the stopping points that later proved necessary added after each branch.

```text
A Nemotron- or Olmo-related exception is reported
|
+-- 1. First ask: at what stage did the exception occur?
|   |
|   +-- Before model type resolution, model selection, or obtaining the constructor
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- Record the model type, configuration snippet, and actual call entry point
|   |   |   +-- Do not open the Olmo2 test as a substitute for this entry point
|   |   |   `-- If the entry point cannot be located, stop attributing a cause and retain only the symptoms
|   |
|   +-- During model loading
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Distinguish between file retrieval, opening weights, and object creation
|   |   +-- On the Olmo side, you can go to the loading section of the olmo2 test
|   |   `-- On the Nemotron side, first find the construction or test location actually involved for Nemotron itself
|   |
|   +-- The model instance has been created, and an exception occurs during execution
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Record the input shapes, the first failure location, and whether there has already been any output
|   |   +-- Do not record a subsequent cleanup timeout as an execution failure
|   |   `-- Reduce the input only if the issue is reproducible
|   |
|   `-- An exception occurs during release or destruction
|       |
|       +-- Track this separately as the cleanup stage
|       `-- Do not go back and change the model mapping to address release issues
|
`-- 2. Keep separate records for Nemotron and Olmo
    |
    +-- Olmo: the Olmo2 test can be used as a local entry point
    `-- Nemotron: wait for the actual file or call location involved
```

## First, Clarify the Symptoms

"Exception boundaries" here is not the name of an error category. It refers to several boundaries that must not be crossed during troubleshooting: between the model directory and a specific constructor, between loading and execution, between execution and release, and between Olmo's existing test entry points and Nemotron's unknown entry points. If a report only says "model failure", it is easy to later combine outputs from different stages into a single issue.

When a record comes in, start by noting just four brief details: whether a model instance had already been obtained before the error appeared; whether an execution run had already started; whether there was any output; whether the test or call reached the release stage. Without these four details, do not guess the stage based on the model name. They are not intended to form a complete incident report, but to prevent a loading failure from being treated as an execution failure, or a timeout during release from being interpreted as the model not being supported.

If the caller can identify the model type or constructor entry point, record the type name and entry point location exactly as provided. Do not fill in registry relationships based on names when no entry point is available. Nemotron and Olmo may all be mentioned before model selection, but "being mentioned" does not mean selection is complete.

If the caller provides only a test name, first confirm whether the test name corresponds to a model, processor, tokenizer, or shared initialization. A name containing Olmo does not necessarily mean the failure occurred in the model object itself; likewise, a name containing Nemotron does not establish that the exception came from the model directory. First find the first section of code actually entered, then use the name as a supporting clue.

## Olmo entry points

`packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js` is the currently visible location of the Olmo2 test. The file imports directly from `../../../src/transformers.js`:

```js
import { GPT2Tokenizer, Olmo2ForCausalLM } from "../../../src/transformers.js";
```

This import answers a very narrow question: at this location, the test file uses both `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM`. It cannot, on its own, answer which model was ultimately selected at runtime, which files were loaded, or whether a particular exception was caused by the tokenizer. Therefore, when troubleshooting, do not copy the import list into a model support matrix.

For Olmo reports, the first step is to check whether the exception occurred before or after these imported objects were used. If the test could not proceed around import or initialization, record that location and the full error message; do not start by reducing the generation input. Only if the model object has already been created should you proceed to examine the execution section. If execution has returned but the test gets stuck at release, switch to the cleanup branch, do not go back and change the assumptions about model selection.

The file also gets these time limits and default options from `../../init.js`:

```js
import {
  MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME,
  MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME,
  MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME,
  DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS,
} from "../../init.js";
```

The names of these three time limits define stage boundaries, not the causes of exceptions. `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME` is only suitable for marking the wait limit during loading; `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME` is suitable for marking the execution boundary after the model starts working; `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` reminds us that release comes after execution. When a particular test takes a long time, first check which boundary it is near. Do not attribute it directly to model loading just because the total runtime is long.

`DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` should also be retained in the record as the fact that "the test defaults were used this time"; do not expand this on your own into a parameter list that was not observed. When options need to be compared, use the overrides visible at the actual call site as the basis. If there are no overrides, do not write that a particular switch caused the difference.

The Olmo branch can be handled in the following order:

1. Confirm whether the record refers to the Olmo or Olmo2 test entry point. The two must not be automatically interchanged on this page.
2. Open `test_modeling_olmo2.js`, and first find where the imported object is first used in testing.
3. Mark whether the anomaly occurs during model loading, during test execution, or before resource release.
4. If tokenization results are involved, separately note whether `GPT2Tokenizer` has already been used; do not assume it is the cause just because it appears in the import list.
5. If a model object is involved, separately note whether `Olmo2ForCausalLM` has finished being created.
6. Only when the issue can be reproduced consistently at the same stage should you continue narrowing it down with smaller input or a single test case.

Step 4 and Step 5 cannot be merged into "model initialization." The case where the tokenizer has been called but the model has not yet been created and the case where the first execution fails after model creation are two different troubleshooting paths. Mixing them into one will make subsequent records unable to show which object was actually reached.

### Olmo loading section

If the anomaly appears in the loading section, first confirm whether model object creation has started. The test file is known to import `Olmo2ForCausalLM`, but the import statement itself is not evidence that creation succeeded. In the record, you can write stage assessments such as "reached the import point," "entered the loading call," or "failed after object creation"; do not compress all three into "loading failed."

If the anomaly occurs before the model object is obtained, retain the call entry point and error; do not change the timeout constant in the test. The timeout constant is merely a boundary on the test side and cannot prove which part of upstream selection, file reading, or object creation went wrong.

If object creation starts but does not complete, still classify it as loading. At this point, do not reduce the execution input to the minimum, because execution has not started. If the default options were changed for troubleshooting, the record must separate "original default options" from "temporary overrides"; otherwise, later results cannot determine whether they are the same as the original issue.

If a load stops around `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME`, this only indicates that the loading section crossed that test boundary. It does not mean that any one of the network, weights, cache, or constructor has been confirmed. When continuing the investigation, follow only the objects actually traversed by the current call; do not list all storage, transport, or cache implementations that were not exercised as candidates on this page.

### Olmo execution section

Only after the object has been created does the execution stage begin. At this point, retain only the minimum input characteristics: whether the input is empty, whether it is a single item, and whether the first failure occurred before any output was produced. Do not add Sequence Length, a device, filename, or return value just to make the record look complete; when these details did not appear in the actual run, stating them precisely will only mislead the next reproduction.

If `GPT2Tokenizer` has completed its local work while execution of `Olmo2ForCausalLM` still has not returned, record "tokenizer passed" and "model execution has not returned" separately. The former narrows the current path; the latter still does not indicate whether the problem is in model computation, input preparation, or the call wrapper.

If an execution result has already appeared and a failure occurs only afterward during end processing, return to the release branch. Do not rewrite an execution stage that has already succeeded as "unstable." A successful execution and a failed release can occur in the same run; retain them as two separate facts.

`MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME` is used to identify the boundary of the test execution stage. When it is exceeded, record which test step was actually entered and whether any output already exists. Do not merge it with `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME` into a single "model timeout"; doing so will lose the most useful stage information.

### Olmo release stage

Resource release occurs after model execution. If an exception occurs during or around release or destruction, first confirm whether any execution output exists, then check whether cleanup has just begun. Since the test file uses `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` separately, the record should likewise retain this stage as a separate line.

When an exception occurs during the release stage, do not modify the model mapping, replace the tokenizer, or replace the model constructor with one for a different model just to get a one-off pass. Those actions change earlier stages and obscure execution that had already completed. You can first reduce the test to a single case that completes the release stage; if a single test case still cannot identify the specific cleanup location, stop at "release-stage exception" and wait for the actual call location.

## Nemotron entry point

The most common mistake when recording Nemotron and Olmo together is to put Nemotron into the same test case simply after seeing the Olmo2 test. Existing materials do not provide Nemotron's corresponding test file, import declaration, or specific call edge. Therefore, the starting point for Nemotron must be the model selection, constructor, or test location actually implicated by the report, not a copy of the Olmo2 test configuration.

If a Nemotron report is received, first distinguish between the following two situations:

- The report provides the model type, constructor name, or call location: use that location to determine whether the problem occurs before selection, during loading, during execution, or during release.
- The report only says "Nемotron exception" and provides no actual location: record only the symptom and environment differences; do not escalate it to an Olmo2 regression or claim that a runnable minimal test case already exists.

Here, "environment differences" refers only to differences that can be directly observed, such as whether the same record used a prerelease package, whether it was a test call or an application call, and whether it reached the release stage. Without actual values, do not append a version number, runner, or platform name. A prerelease version by itself is not a common cause.
If Nemotron fails before model selection, the current top priority is to preserve the model type and the entry point through which the request arrived. At this stage, there is still no reason to move into Olmo's model tests. If selection is complete but construction is not, continue tracing the path Nemotron actually hit; still do not replace it with the creation process for `Olmo2ForCausalLM`.

If Nemotron has completed creation and fails during execution, record the minimal characteristics of the input and whether output has started. If it subsequently fails only during resource release, log it under the cleanup phase. Even if the phase names match Olmo's, the two sides should retain separate reproduction entries; what they share is a classification scheme, not evidence.

The stopping condition for the Nemotron branch applies earlier than Olmo's: if there is no location actually reached locally, do not continue guessing about model files, tokenizers, configuration fields or public storage. You can leave a follow-up item after the exception record: a construction or test entry point that is actually reached is needed. Do not disguise this follow-up item as a verified regression conclusion.

## Correction to the Early Consolidation Assessment

The original record worded "Nemotron and Olmo are all within the exception boundary" in a way that made them sound too closely related, making it easy to read them as the same class of defect. That assessment is retained for the purpose it served at the time: when scattered pre-release issues arose, the on-call staff would at least not overlook the two names. The approach is now revised as follows:

- The two model names can be used together as search clues.
- The Olmo2 test file serves only localized follow-up investigation on the Olmo side.
- Nemotron must first find the entry point it actually enters.
- If an exception has no phase recorded, add the phase first; if it has no entry point, stop at the missing entry point for now.

This does not remove Nemotron from the scope of investigation, but removes it from an unverified shared path. If the two sides are later found to share the same call site, a shared branch can be established at that location; until then, similar symptoms must not be used to merge evidence.

## Handling Order

The following sequence applies to a new report. It deliberately does not require running every item; first, just place the current exception in a branch that will not mislead anyone.

**A. First identify the model side.** If the report explicitly identifies Olmo, enter the Olmo branch; if it explicitly identifies Nemotron, enter the Nemotron branch; if it only refers generically to a model exception, do not attribute it to either side. When the model side is unclear, first find the call entry point, rather than picking a seemingly similar case from the test directory.

**B. Then identify the phase.** Prefer the four categories "before selection, loading, execution, release". Before selection covers model type parsing, selection and the period before obtaining a constructor; loading runs from the start of model creation until the model object is usable; execution runs from when the object is usable until output exists or execution returns; release runs from the start of cleanup until resources have been released. If the boundary is not yet clear, you can write "undetermined between loading/execution", but must not force it into a category.

**C. Finally decide whether to narrow it down.** Only when both the model side and the phase are known is it worth narrowing down to a single test case. For Olmo's loading, execution and release, you can continue investigating through the existing objects in the test file; for Nemotron, narrow it down only when a location actually hit is already available. The goal of narrowing down is to confirm the phase, not to get a successful run on a different path as quickly as possible.

**D. Wrap up the record.** You can stop once you have the phase, the entry point, and the original error. If an entry point is missing, state the gap specifically: Nemotron's actual test or construction entry point has not yet been located; or the first failure point within the Olmo2 test has not yet been located. Do not replace these two distinct gaps with a generic "pending further analysis".

## Common wrong turns

### Treating a successful import as proof that the model is usable

The fact that `test_modeling_olmo2.js` can import `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM` does not mean that the test has finished creating the model object, nor does it mean that execution succeeded. After the import completes, the process may still get stuck during loading, execution, or release. If the record only says "import is fine", the next person handling it still will not know the failure phase.

The correction is to add the first actual failure point after the import. If that point cannot be obtained, keep "not located after import"; do not upgrade it to "model is usable".

### Treating a test time limit as the root cause

The three time limits correspond to loading, execution, and release, respectively. They help identify the phase, but do not identify the cause. This is especially true of `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME`: when this boundary is reached, the preceding model execution may already have completed. Classifying it as model loading will direct subsequent changes to the wrong place.

The correction is to first check the last completed phase. If creation has completed, no longer call it "unable to load"; if output has been obtained, no longer call it "unable to execute". Describe the remaining problem according to its actual phase.

### Directly reusing the Olmo2 test case for Nemotron

This is the most dangerous shortcut in the early records. The Olmo2 file is an existing local entry point, not a universal fixture for all language models. Copying that test case for Nemotron, even if it produces new results, cannot establish that it follows the same path as the original Nemotron exception.

The correction is to first locate where Nemotron is actually reached. If it cannot be found, stop; do not borrow Olmo2's imports, time limits, or default options to manufacture a conclusion. You can put Olmo's investigation record and Nemotron's record awaiting localization on the same page, but they must remain two separate tracks.

### Recasting a release problem as an execution problem

When a model call has already returned and a resource cleanup exception occurs afterward, the easiest approach is often to retain only the final failure text. This loses the counterevidence that "execution has already completed". For prerelease regression testing, this distinction affects whether to examine the model path or shutdown handling.

The correction is to write down two short conclusions together: whether execution returned; whether release completed. Do not let the latter overwrite the former just to keep the wording concise.

### Changing the default options before confirming the original problem

`DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` is the source of the default options currently used by the test file. Changing it directly without first preserving the original option state only produces a run result under different conditions. Especially when the boundary between loading and execution is unclear, this may make the original exception disappear without establishing that the problem has been fixed.

The correction is to run the original call first, then make one localized change within the same phase. If the problem disappears after the change, you can only record that "the temporary override changed the result"; unless you can identify the actual overridden option and the phase, do not state a definitive cause.

## Short notes to leave while on call

The following sentences can be selected as appropriate on site; they do not all need to be filled in:

- "Olmo2: Model import has been reached; whether object creation was entered has not been confirmed."
- "Olmo2: The object has been created; the execution segment has not returned; release has not started."
- "Olmo2: Execution output already exists; the failure occurred in the cleanup segment."
- "Nemotron: The report did not provide the actual call entry point, and the issue was not reproduced using the Olmo2 case."
- "Nemotron: The process was located before model selection; construction has not started."
- "Nemotron: Construction has started; subsequent stages await confirmation against the actual entry point."

These records are meant to preserve boundaries, not replace the original error. The original error should still be stored together with the corresponding call site. If there is only a verbal description and no entry point, the short record can initially be filed under Nemotron or Olmo, but do not provide a constructor, file, or failure cause.

## Order for checking Olmo2 files

When opening `packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js`, there is no need to read the entire test file in one pass. Just stop at the following points in order:

1. First inspect the usage points of `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM` to confirm which object was involved in the symptom for that run.
2. Next check whether the test uses `DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS`, and whether there is a local override visible at the call site.
3. Compare `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME`, `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME`, and `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` to determine which stage was completed last.
4. If there was no model object before the failure, do not continue examining the execution input.
5. If execution has already ended, do not retroactively record the exception as a loading issue.
6. If only incomplete release remains, record the cleanup segment separately; do not expand it into a model support conclusion.

This order is more reliable than inferring the model name from the error text. The test file provides a specific Olmo2 observation point; it is not responsible for proving the entire model directory.

## Parallel handling of two types of reports

Sometimes an exception description for Nemotron and Olmo is received in the same round. In that case, one stage table can be shared, but the results must not be shared:

| Model side | Available entry point | Confirm first | Materials that must not be borrowed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Olmo | `test_modeling_olmo2.js` | The first test stage entered after import | Nemotron's construction or execution conclusions |
| Nemotron | The location actually hit in the report | Whether model selection has been completed | Olmo2's test results and default options |

The "available entry point" in the table does not mean that Olmo is already fully covered. It only means that there is currently a path that can be revisited. When no files are listed for Nemotron, do not fill in the blank with any seemingly plausible directory.

Even if both types of reports show timeouts, still separate them by stage first. Olmo stopping at the loading boundary and Nemotron stopping at the execution boundary are different symptoms; even if neither produces output, they should not be merged into the same issue. Conversely, if both have completed execution and stop only during release, the "cleanup stage" can be noted as a shared observation, but their respective entry points must still be retained.

## When to stop

In the following situations, stop narrowing things down rather than fabricating explanations:

- No construction, call, or test location has actually been found for Nemotron.
- The Olmo records can only confirm the import, not the first failure after the import.
- The original exception does not indicate whether a model object was ever created.
- The test only shows the total elapsed time and does not indicate whether it stopped during loading, execution, or release.
- The default options were temporarily changed, but the original conditions were not recorded.

Stopping does not mean the error has gone away. It means the current material only supports going as far as this boundary. For Olmo, the next time raw output is available, continue from the actual point of use of `test_modeling_olmo2.js`; for Nemotron, first recover the actual entry point before proceeding with model-side troubleshooting.

## Follow-up notes

If follow-up records need to be added, do not rewrite all the branches on this page. Add only one line under the corresponding model and stage: the file or call location actually found, the last successful stage, the first failure location, and whether release was entered. If the results overturn an earlier assessment, retain the old assessment and mark beside it that it no longer applies, and in particular do not reintroduce the old shortcut "Olmo2 is the entry point for Nemotron."

There are currently only two items still missing: Nemotron's locally identified entry point, and a captured sample from the Olmo2 tests that can reliably indicate the stage of the first failure. Continue handling the remaining branches according to the stage breakdown above.

# CLI Parsing Trial Plan

For this round of interface review, proceed on the assumption that the parsing layer will not grow into a separate subsystem. CLI is responsible only for collecting command-line values; object construction will still go through the existing entry point. Otherwise, prerelease testing will have two sets of defaults and two error paths, making it hard for regression testing to determine whether differences come from argument interpretation or processor loading.

The place available for a lightweight check is `packages/transformers/tests/models/jina_clip/test_processor_jina_clip.js`. The file directly imports `AutoProcessor`, `JinaCLIPProcessor` and `load_cached_image`, and uses `MAX_PROCESSOR_LOAD_TIME` and `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME`. This looks more like a processor test, so it should not be used as grounds for classifying CLI under JinaCLIP; however, we can reuse its loading time limit to first observe whether command-line arguments introduce extra waiting in the processor initialization path.

Start by trying two narrow paths: one that passes only explicit model or resource arguments, and one that uses defaults throughout. Pass the parsed result as a plain object to the existing entry point, without adding model-type branches in this layer. Callers are responsible for avoiding mutually exclusive arguments for now; if constraints on argument combinations are actually needed later, consider adding group definitions in the parsing layer then.

Rollback criteria: if the default and explicit paths select different processors, or the parsing layer starts duplicating resource cache logic, stop using this approach and return to handling each entry point separately.

To confirm: who maintains the help text; whether exceptions should be raised unchanged or rewritten at CLI.

# CLI Parsing Trial Plan

The original idea was to keep the command-line layer very thin: read options and pass them to the existing loading entry point, without making it understand model directories, processor implementations, or resource caches. That reasoning has been kept because it explains why a separate argument object was not introduced right away. But it also oversimplified one thing: "thin" does not mean that all arguments can be combined freely.

## Trade-offs from the Initial Draft

The initial draft used `packages/transformers/tests/models/jina_clip/test_processor_jina_clip.js` as a temporary observation point. The direct imports visible in that file are:

```js
import { AutoProcessor, JinaCLIPProcessor } from "../../../src/transformers.js";
import { load_cached_image } from "../../asset_cache.js";
import { MAX_PROCESSOR_LOAD_TIME, MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME } from "../../init.js";
```

The assumption at the time was that, as long as the result of CLI still ultimately went through `AutoProcessor`, we could reuse the processor-loading time limit to check for differences. That assumption did not receive enough support later: this test sits alongside the JinaCLIP processor and image resources; it is not an implementation description that can stand in for the CLI entry point. The old plan remains here because several discussions have continued to rely on the claim that "processor tests can cover parsing." Deleting it would make the later disagreements look as though they came out of nowhere.

The narrower conclusion is worth keeping: handling parsed values should not involve reimplementing resource reads at the CLI layer, nor should processors be preloaded just to display help text. `load_cached_image` stays in the test and resource paths; it must not become part of the CLI's default behavior.

## Revised Trial Approach After Review

The creation notes for HFJ-217 require checking CLI Parsing in an environment without old caches or personal configuration, and recording which paths were created and which were not. The card also lists `add_argument`, `add_mutually_exclusive_group`, and `afmoe` as search variants. The follow-up only confirmed that the card already had an owner; it left no record linking these three names into a single implementation chain.

The trial therefore no longer aims to "cover processor loading." Instead, it starts by examining the argument declarations themselves. The first batch allows only two kinds of declarations: single-value options and explicitly mutually exclusive option groups. Single-value options are registered through `add_argument`; when two values cannot appear together, use `add_mutually_exclusive_group`. This does not mean writing a CLI branch for every model type. The point is to avoid quietly turning argument names into aliases for the model registry.

The proposed call shape is limited to this layer:

```js
const parser = new ArgumentParser();
parser.add_argument("--model");
const source = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group();
const options = parser.parse_args();
```

The snippet above indicates the intended interface, not code that has been implemented. In particular, `afmoe` should not be used as the default value for any argument; it is only a search term on the card, not a default model that this proposal can confirm. The initial draft leaned toward putting model types directly into the parsing layer. That part should now be treated as a discarded working assumption.

One earlier constraint still applies during the trial: without old caches or personal configuration, cases with explicitly supplied values and cases with omitted values must be recorded separately. Record the shape of the parsed object and whether the loading entry point was reached; do not use processor execution time as a substitute for parsing results. If a default value appears only through personal configuration, first treat its source as unclear rather than baking it into the help text.

## Two Approaches Not Adopted

One approach is to have CLI recognize all model types directly, then select a processor or model constructor. It looks like it saves steps in a demo, but it would require corresponding changes to the command-line layer whenever the registry is extended. The available material does not establish that this layer can maintain that mapping over the long term. The other approach is to declare no mutual exclusion at all and leave conflicts for downstream errors to report. The initial draft favored this approach because it required the fewest changes when there were few arguments. After review, it is no longer recommended: once conflicting values reach the loading entry point, the failure we see no longer tells us exactly what the user passed.

Keeping mutually exclusive groups means the help output must be updated when group membership changes, and callers must decide which options really are mutually exclusive. This costs less than maintaining a table of model types, but it is not free. Use it only for arguments with established conflicts; unconfirmed combinations remain two ordinary options.

## Withdrawal and Outstanding Items

If the parsing layer starts reading caches, loading images, or constructing `JinaCLIPProcessor` to determine default values, this trial approach is to be withdrawn. If mutually exclusive groups cannot express the actual argument relationships, do not force a fit with multiple levels of nested groups. Fall back to single-value declarations and leave conflict handling to code closer to the business logic entry point.

The unresolved issue is not syntax but ownership of default values: should CLI fill them in, or should the downstream entry point? The review so far only narrows the question to these two places; it cannot decide between them.

# Documentation Site Postmortem: Two States of the Same Object

The documentation site's docs and guide originally served together as the user entry point, with version notes and outdated content handled under the same maintenance arrangement. During verification, the same "transformers · User Documentation Portal" object showed different current revisions at two points in time. The two sets of content were not treated as separate objects; during the investigation, they were first saved as two states of the same object.

This first came to light when the ONNX manifest did not match the old record. The old record was still accessible, and the landing page still pointed to usable content, so it initially looked more like a delayed manifest update or version notes that had not been cleared out somewhere. That assessment did not hold up: on another check, the conflict was not confined to one line in the manifest. The current entry point itself supplied a different current revision for the same object.

## Sequence of observations

1. The old record came first. It preserved the state of the documentation site's entry point at the time and included the version information used for comparison with the ONNX manifest.
2. A different current revision was then observed through the current entry point. The two records had the same object name; renaming could not be used to treat them as separate objects.
3. No further repeated requests were made to the entry point during the investigation. The original record was retained, and the recovery page was kept separately to prevent later entry-point changes from overwriting the initial discrepancy.
4. The runtime version was later restored. This recovery only showed that the version field could be returned to a usable state; it did not mean that the cause of the partial content changes across the two instances had been found.

For a while, the work focused on "was the old manifest out of sync?" This was a working hypothesis at the time, not a confirmed cause. The old manifest was indeed where the problem first surfaced, but it could not explain why two current revisions appeared for the same object at two points in time. The review therefore did not list services outside the documentation site, build processes, or neighboring projects as causes.

## Impact

The first impact was on maintenance decisions for the documentation site: someone viewing the entry point could not determine which revision to use from the "current" label alone. The inconsistent entry-point states also meant that version notes and the handling of outdated content could not be finalized immediately. The old record was not invalid; it documented a state that had actually appeared at an earlier point in time. Nor was the recovery page a replacement for the old record; it only preserved what could be confirmed during recovery.

There was no evidence that all docs or guide content had been affected in the same way. The documentation site had its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria, but this record did not turn those management boundaries into technical causes. In particular, when both items were missing, the entry-point names alone were not enough to infer that they pointed to the same underlying content; this remained unknown during the investigation.

## Preservation and stopping point

The materials retained at the time were located at `docs/adj-transformers/incidents/transformers-user-documentation-portal-two-states-for-one-object.md`. They should include the original record, the recovery page, and a record of the unconfirmed cause—not just the runtime version restored later. The reason was straightforward: if the entry point changed again, the initially observed state could still be distinguished from the later recovery state.

Further retries were stopped, not because the discrepancy had disappeared, but because continuing to read the same entry point would not fill two critical gaps: when each of the different current revisions appeared, and why the partial content changed. Without those two points in time, any new page retrieved later could only constitute a new state; it could not retrospectively explain the original observations.

The reviewer checked again through the original entry point and confirmed only that a discrepancy existed between the current entry point and the saved old record; no conclusions were drawn for branches that had not been reproduced. The inconsistency in the ONNX manifest remained at the start of the timeline because it explained why verification began, but it was no longer treated as the sole cause.

## Open questions

- The timing information for when the two current revisions appeared is still incomplete.
- The reason for the change in partial content has not been confirmed.
- The existing records are insufficient to determine whether the runtime version recovery was related to the entry-point state switch.

If new original records are obtained later, append them after this event and clearly state which point in time each corresponds to; do not overwrite old records or backfill the first observation with the post-recovery entry-point state.

versions.body:
# Resource Site Approach Not Adopted

At the time, we wanted to pull `transformers-documentation-portal` out from alongside the existing docs and guide entry points and make it a standalone entry point for users. The idea wasn't to replace the content, but to bring release notes, handling of outdated content, and user entry points into the same release workflow. That way, readers wouldn't first have to guess whether a section of the guide still matched the version they were looking at; maintainers could also flag old content that should be retired when release notes appeared.

We ultimately didn't adopt this approach. The issue wasn't whether the pages could be built. Once the resource site became an entry point in its own right, we would first have to answer two unresolved questions: would the old docs remain a user entry point or serve only as an index, and would the existing release notes in guide move or coexist in two places? The former would leave people used to the old entry point suddenly unable to find content, while the latter would leave maintainers manually keeping track of which notes were still valid. At the time, we weren't confident that the latter would be low-cost.

We made a preliminary comparison of two options:

- **Standalone resource site approach**: The resource site would handle user entry points, release notes, and notices about outdated content; docs and guide would remain content sources. The benefit would be organizing entry points centrally by version; the cost would be checking where links on both sides pointed after every content change.
- **Keep the existing entry points**: Continue filling in the missing information in docs and guide, leaving only navigation and an archive location for the resource site. This wouldn't solve the problem of scattered entry points, but it wouldn't introduce a new layer of navigation before the content had stabilized.

At the time, we leaned toward the latter, so we didn't schedule implementation of the standalone resource site. That judgment rested on one assumption: the existing entry points could still handle the volume of changes to the release notes. If the same set of notes needed updating separately in docs, guide, and the resource site, or if retiring old content required manual page-by-page tracking, that assumption would no longer hold. At that point, we would reverse the decision to "hold off on splitting it out" and reopen discussion of a trial for the standalone entry point.

If the trial is reopened, start with only a small section of content that already has release notes, rather than migrating the entire guide. Watch whether the resource site actually reduces how often readers have to go back and forth between entry points to decide where to look, and whether old content can be clearly flagged when versions change. The resource site must not become just another copy of the content; if it only adds a layer of links, stop the trial.

Still undecided:

- Whether the old docs would still count as the main user entry point after the resource site appears;
- Whether outdated content should stay in place with a notice or move into the archive;
- Whether content maintainers should enter release notes into the resource site, or the notes should be compiled during resource site maintenance.

The original draft is still at `docs/adj-transformers/proposals/rejected-transformers-user-documentation-portal-approach.md`. This record preserves the trade-offs behind the approach not adopted at the time and the conditions for reversing that decision. Any later entry-point arrangements should be recorded separately, rather than retroactively presented as conclusions already reached in this discussion.

## Path Not Taken

If you haven't obtained the next page's body, record the current page and the reason for stopping; that makes it easier to reconstruct what happened on the next review than filling the gap with descriptions from adjacent projects.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Package Integration

Start with the first visible symptom at the entry point, not by guessing at long-term causes. This covers the cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integration between `packages`. Follow only the names and sequence that actually appear; stop any branch at its current node when evidence is missing.

## Preserve the state first

Open `docs/adj-generation-state/runbooks/generation-state-package-integration-blocked-escalation-contacts.md` and start with the records around `hub fetch`. First, save the first failing sample, `model type`, `runtime version`, the version combination, and whether `ONNX manifest` appeared. Preserve the cache directory as well. The older records include one premature retry. Retrying changes the sequence before and after the first failure, so do not clear the cache first or treat post-retry output as the original result.

If there is no `hub fetch` at the entry point, stop at the entry-point record. At this point, you can only confirm that this section was not reached in the current record; you cannot determine whether the stall is in consumer integration, the cross-package version combination, or an in-package call that has not yet continued. If `hub fetch` is visible at the entry point, check the next point for `FileCache`.

## Branches

### `hub fetch` is followed by `FileCache`

First, check whether the record contains `model type`.

- Absent: Stop. Do not infer the model type from the filename or use `release note` in place of a run result. Send the entry-point location and the first failing sample to the package maintenance intake; if the attachment or the record itself is unreadable, route it to the permissions owner instead.
- Present: Check whether `ONNX manifest` appears in the same attempt. The names, version combination, and consumer integration must each be saved based on this attempt's record; do not merge same-named symptoms from adjacent packages into a single entry.
- `ONNX manifest` absent: Stop at this checklist item. You can only confirm that it is absent from the saved record; this does not establish whether the cache is invalid, the versions are incompatible, or the consumer has not completed integration.
- `ONNX manifest` present: Record only the first actual output after it. If there is no subsequent output, stop; do not perform another unrecorded recovery action just to get through the tree.

### `FileCache` did not appear

Do not go straight back to the model-name branch. Preserve the objects already present at the entry point and their order, then verify whether `hub fetch` actually completed and whether `runtime version` was saved with the sample. If either is missing, end this branch here; someone who can read that entry point or attachment must supply the missing information. The available material does not support interpreting "`FileCache` was not seen" as a package integration failure.

### No `Qwen2VL` in the record

An older branch used "`Qwen2VL` did not appear" as a stopping point. Retain that assessment of the observed state here, but it only means the name is absent from this record, not that the model is necessarily unsupported or that `generation-state-package-integration` has failed. Look back at `model type` and `ONNX manifest`: if neither provides new evidence, do not speculate further; route to the permissions owner or package maintenance intake and preserve the original record.

### Still stalled even though `Qwen2VL` appears

Do not broaden the investigation to other model names. Verify that `runtime version` and the failing sample belong to the same attempt, then confirm that the version combination and consumer integration can be matched within the same record. If any item is missing, stop the branch here; if you have read access but there is no new call output, pass it to the maintenance intake for that `packages` combination. If permissions are insufficient, route only to the permissions owner; do not infer an internal package cause from a permissions issue.

## Exit actions

Failing sample available: Preserve the sample, environment differences, cache directory, and entry-point location, and stop retrying. No failing sample: Stop and state which item is missing; do not write recovery commands. This record contains no rollback command validated in a shared environment, so untested actions must not be listed as steps. The temporary assignee is to handle only actions that are due, not supply a long-term interpretation on behalf of Generation state · Package Integration.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Review

During this maintenance window, the results shown by the team's public entry point did not match the original plan. The first thing observed was a discrepancy at the entry point, not an error in model loading itself; the incident notes initially linked the two too closely. That assessment is retained here to distinguish what was observable at the time from the actions later taken to restore visible results.

After the window started, maintenance proceeded as planned. When the issue was first noticed, the public entry point's results had not switched as planned. All that could be confirmed at the time was that the entry point's results were abnormal; it was not clear whether the issue lay in the model mapping, entry point configuration, or remnants of the old path. No signal was observed that could isolate any one of these three as the cause, so the entry point discrepancy was not recorded as an established runtime failure.

The model mapping diff from that time was then retrieved for comparison. The diff showed that the planned changes had indeed occurred, and that material had been available during the incident for later review; it did not explain why the public entry point was still returning the old results. The original notes treated the diff as the closest lead to the anomaly. It was later recognized that this conflated "the change exists" with "the entry point selected the change." The notes remain on file in their original context.

The temporary response did not expand the mapping changes further. Instead, the old entry point was retained to restore visible results. The old entry point could be withdrawn, so this was an on-call recovery action, not confirmation of the mapping diff. After recovery, the same entry point no longer produced results that conflicted with the plan. The impact record was also limited to the public entry point layer; it was not used to infer that the model directory or runtime behavior had been affected.

During incident coordination, the record was split into three parts: the entry point behavior first observed, the old entry point retained to restore results, and the mapping diff, which could explain only part of the situation. This keeps handoffs from recording the recovery time as the point when the root cause became known, or mistaking the old entry point's presence for a long-term choice. If the same discrepancy appears again, first check the results actually returned by the entry point, then decide whether the diff needs to be reviewed.

Still unknown: why the old entry point continued to participate in result selection during the maintenance window; whether the discrepancy occurs only in this kind of public entry point maintenance; and whether it will recur after the temporary entry point is withdrawn. The original notes leaned toward classifying the issue as a mapping change that had not taken effect. That was the working assessment at the time, with insufficient evidence, and cannot serve as a conclusion for subsequent handling.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

This answer retains the early wording about the entry point because many old discussions left only the judgment that "the entry point is still there." That judgment is useful for locating a candidate path, not for endorsing it; don't conflate what's displayed at the public entry point with a complete review.

The entry point here is more of a shared lookup location than a place to store results. It can show whether a candidate path is still referenced and whether its name is still available for discussion, but it doesn't combine baseline behavior, post-fix behavior, and post-withdrawal behavior into one record. For that reason, the old statement "the entry point is still there, so it has already been integrated" remains available as historical wording, but can no longer be used to close items.

**What does the existing generation-state entry point prove?**

It proves that maintainers still have a shared lookup location: the candidate path hasn't disappeared from the entry point, and its name is still available for discussion. The earlier answer described this step as "already integrated and ready to close." A later on-site review found that this skipped the fix and withdrawal stages. The existence of the entry point is neither a record of baseline behavior nor a record that the fix has taken effect.

If all we confirm is that the name at the entry point hasn't changed, we can at most confirm that the candidate is still listed at the public entry point. We also need to run the same input through the existing path and the modified path to compare their actual behavior; checking again after withdrawal confirms that the entry point text is no longer endorsing the change. When results haven't been recorded separately for all three stages, this page does not interpret entry point status as completion status.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

The old draft said, "The entry point maintainer just needs to withdraw it." That statement has no supporting basis and is retained as historical wording. Only two things have been confirmed: the party proposing the candidate path must explain the reason for withdrawal, and the entry point maintainer must also handle the reference at the entry point. There is no conclusion here on whether the same person performs both actions or who makes the final decision in a dispute. The entry point remaining visible does not mean someone has taken over responsibility for withdrawal.

So the party proposing the candidate path cannot leave only the word "withdrawn," nor can they treat a missing reason as a decision by the entry point maintainer. The entry point maintainer handles the reference at the public entry point; the proposing party records the reason for withdrawal. The available records do not establish that both actions must be performed by the same person, nor do they identify an alternate decision-maker in a dispute.

**Under what conditions can the item be closed?**

The team's established practice is: only when the same input has produced reviewable results on the baseline, fixed, and rollback paths may the responsible person move the card into the release window. "The same input" is intended to prevent each stage from using a different sample and leaving conclusions that only appear consistent. The baseline preserves the original behavior, the fix records behavior after the change, and the rollback path confirms that removing the change hasn't left the judgment in the entry point text.

If any one of these three results is missing, checking the entry point can only serve as a lookup, not as a closure action. In particular, when the entry point text has already been changed, we still need to check whether the rollback path brings back the old judgment; the absence of the old wording on the page does not mean rollback is complete. Review results remain the basis for closure, rather than prematurely reducing that basis to what's displayed at the entry point.
